ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.title: Proximal points and the subgradient optimality condition
ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.summary:
Throughout this section \(E\) is a real inner-product space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) and norm \(\|\cdot\|\), \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is a real-valued function and \(\lambda>0\). The proximal objective at an input \(x\in E\) is \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\), and a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) is a global minimizer of \(Q_{\lambda,x}\). A subgradient of \(f\) at \(p\) is a vector \(s\) such that the affine function \(y\mapsto f(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\) lies below \(f\) on all of \(E\).

We prove: (i) subgradients are monotone; (ii) \(p\) is a proximal point at \(x\) whenever the scaled residual \((x-p)/\lambda\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(p\), and, for convex \(f\), conversely; (iii) for convex \(f\), proximal points satisfy the firm nonexpansiveness inequality \(\|p-q\|^2\le\langle x-y,p-q\rangle\), so they are unique and both \(x\mapsto p\) and \(x\mapsto x-p\) are \(1\)-Lipschitz; (iv) if \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(f\) is convex and bounded below, a proximal point exists at every input. The proximal map \(P_\lambda\) is then the map sending \(x\) to its unique proximal point.

These facts are used for the Moreau envelope in the next section, whose gradient is \((x-P_\lambda(x))/\lambda\), for the energy inequalities of the pairwise proximal particle updates, and for the contraction and parameter-sensitivity estimates of the splitting scheme.

steps.title: Proximal objective, proximal points and monotone subgradients
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\), \(\lambda>0\) and \(x\in E\). The proximal objective is

\[Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\qquad(p\in E).\]

A point \(p\in E\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) with parameter \(\lambda\) if \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\) for every \(y\in E\), that is, if \(p\) is a global minimizer of \(Q_{\lambda,x}\). A vector \(s\in E\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(p\), written \(s\in\partial f(p)\), if

\[f(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le f(y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E.\qquad(1)\]

Inequality (1) says that the affine function \(y\mapsto f(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\) lies below \(f\) on all of \(E\) and agrees with \(f\) at \(p\). Neither definition requires convexity or differentiability of \(f\).

Claim (monotonicity of subgradients). Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be any function, let \(p,q\in E\), \(s\in\partial f(p)\) and \(t\in\partial f(q)\). Then

\[\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\ge0.\]

Proof. Apply (1) for \(s\) at \(p\) with \(y=q\), and (1) for \(t\) at \(q\) with \(y=p\):

\[f(p)+\langle s,q-p\rangle\le f(q),\qquad f(q)+\langle t,p-q\rangle\le f(p).\]

Since \(q-p=-(p-q)\), linearity of the inner product in its second argument gives \(\langle s,q-p\rangle=-\langle s,p-q\rangle\). Adding the two inequalities and cancelling the real number \(f(p)+f(q)\) from both sides gives

\[-\langle s,p-q\rangle+\langle t,p-q\rangle\le0.\]

By linearity in the first argument the left-hand side equals \(-\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\). Hence \(\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\ge0\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The residual subgradient condition characterizes proximal points
steps.body:
Recall that \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is convex if \(f((1-t)p+ty)\le(1-t)f(p)+tf(y)\) for all \(p,y\in E\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\).

Claim. Let \(\lambda>0\), \(x,p\in E\) and \(f:E\to\mathbb R\).

  1. (Sufficiency.) If \(\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p)\), then \(p\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\). No convexity of \(f\) is needed.
  2. (Necessity.) If \(f\) is convex and \(p\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\), then \(\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p)\).

Consequently, for convex \(f\) and \(\lambda>0\),

\[p\text{ is a proximal point of }f\text{ at }x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial f(p).\]

Proof of sufficiency. Fix \(y\in E\). Writing \(y-x=(p-x)+(y-p)\) and expanding the squared norm,

\[\|y-x\|^2=\|p-x\|^2+2\langle p-x,y-p\rangle+\|y-p\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

The hypothesis, tested at \(y\), reads \(f(p)+\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\le f(y)\). Since \(\langle x-p,y-p\rangle=-\langle p-x,y-p\rangle\), this is

\[f(y)-f(p)\ge-\frac1\lambda\langle p-x,y-p\rangle.\qquad(2)\]

Using (1) and then (2),

\[\begin{aligned} Q_{\lambda,x}(y)-Q_{\lambda,x}(p)&=f(y)-f(p)+\frac{\|y-x\|^2-\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\\ &=f(y)-f(p)+\frac1\lambda\langle p-x,y-p\rangle+\frac{\|y-p\|^2}{2\lambda}\\ &\ge\frac{\|y-p\|^2}{2\lambda}\ge0 . \end{aligned}\]

Hence \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\); as \(y\) was arbitrary, \(p\) is a proximal point. \(\square\) The computation also gives the quadratic growth \(Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\ge Q_{\lambda,x}(p)+\|y-p\|^2/(2\lambda)\).

Proof of necessity. Fix \(y\in E\). It suffices to show that

\[f(p)+\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\le f(y)+\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0,\]

because a real number that is at most \(f(y)+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\) is at most \(f(y)\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\) and put

\[t=\min\Bigl(1,\ \frac{2\lambda\varepsilon}{\|y-p\|^2+1}\Bigr).\]

Then \(0<t\le1\) and \(t(\|y-p\|^2+1)\le2\lambda\varepsilon\); since \(t>0\), in particular

\[t\|y-p\|^2\le2\lambda\varepsilon.\qquad(3)\]

Let \(y_t=(1-t)p+ty\). Convexity of \(f\) with weights \(1-t\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\) gives

\[f(y_t)\le(1-t)f(p)+tf(y).\qquad(4)\]

Since \(y_t-x=(p-x)+t(y-p)\), expanding the squared norm gives \(\|y_t-x\|^2=\|p-x\|^2+2t\langle p-x,y-p\rangle+t^2\|y-p\|^2\). Minimality of \(p\) gives \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y_t)\); cancelling \(\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\) and applying (4),

\[f(p)\le f(y_t)+\frac{2t\langle p-x,y-p\rangle+t^2\|y-p\|^2}{2\lambda}\le(1-t)f(p)+tf(y)+\frac{t}{\lambda}\langle p-x,y-p\rangle+\frac{t^2}{2\lambda}\|y-p\|^2.\]

Subtracting \((1-t)f(p)\) from both sides and multiplying by \(2\lambda>0\) gives

\[t\Bigl(2\lambda\bigl(f(p)-f(y)\bigr)-2\langle p-x,y-p\rangle-t\|y-p\|^2\Bigr)\le0.\]

Because \(t>0\), the bracket is nonpositive. Dividing the bracket by \(2\lambda>0\) and using (3) divided by \(2\lambda\),

\[f(p)-\frac1\lambda\langle p-x,y-p\rangle\le f(y)+\frac{t\|y-p\|^2}{2\lambda}\le f(y)+\varepsilon.\]

The left-hand side equals \(f(p)+\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\), which proves the reduced claim. \(\square\)

The equivalence is the conjunction of the two implications. The choice of \(t\) replaces the limit \(t\downarrow0\) of the directional-derivative argument by a single admissible value of \(t\) for each \(\varepsilon\).

steps.title: Firm nonexpansiveness and uniqueness of proximal points
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(f\) be convex, \(\lambda>0\), let \(p\) be a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) and \(q\) a proximal point of \(f\) at \(y\), both with parameter \(\lambda\). Then

\[\|p-q\|^2\le\langle x-y,p-q\rangle,\qquad(1)\] \[\|p-q\|\le\|x-y\|,\qquad\|(x-p)-(y-q)\|\le\|x-y\|.\qquad(2)\]

If \(x=y\), then \(p=q\); that is, the proximal point at a given input is unique.

Proof. By the necessity part of the previous step, \(\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p)\) and \(\lambda^{-1}(y-q)\in\partial f(q)\). Monotonicity of subgradients gives

\[0\le\bigl\langle\lambda^{-1}(x-p)-\lambda^{-1}(y-q),\,p-q\bigr\rangle=\lambda^{-1}\bigl\langle(x-p)-(y-q),\,p-q\bigr\rangle.\]

Since \(\lambda^{-1}>0\), \(\langle(x-p)-(y-q),p-q\rangle\ge0\). Writing \((x-p)-(y-q)=(x-y)-(p-q)\) and using \(\langle p-q,p-q\rangle=\|p-q\|^2\), this is \(\langle x-y,p-q\rangle-\|p-q\|^2\ge0\), which is (1).

Uniqueness. If \(x=y\), the right-hand side of (1) is \(\langle0,p-q\rangle=0\). Hence \(\|p-q\|^2\le0\), so \(\|p-q\|=0\) and \(p=q\).

Nonexpansiveness. By (1) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(\langle x-y,p-q\rangle\le\|x-y\|\,\|p-q\|\),

\[\|p-q\|^2\le\|x-y\|\,\|p-q\|.\]

If \(\|p-q\|>\|x-y\|\), then \(\|p-q\|>0\) and multiplying the strict inequality by \(\|p-q\|\) would give \(\|p-q\|^2>\|x-y\|\,\|p-q\|\), a contradiction. Hence \(\|p-q\|\le\|x-y\|\).

Residual nonexpansiveness. Put \(u=x-y\) and \(v=p-q\), so that \((x-p)-(y-q)=u-v\) and (1) reads \(\|v\|^2\le\langle u,v\rangle\). Expanding the square,

\[\|u-v\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\le\|u\|^2-2\|v\|^2+\|v\|^2=\|u\|^2-\|v\|^2\le\|u\|^2.\]

Both norms are nonnegative, so \(\|u-v\|\le\|u\|\), which is the second inequality in (2). \(\square\)

Inequality (1) is the firm nonexpansiveness of the proximal map. By (2), the proximal map \(x\mapsto p\) and the residual map \(x\mapsto x-p\) are both \(1\)-Lipschitz.

steps.title: Existence of proximal points and the proximal map
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be convex and bounded below, say \(f(z)\ge b\) for all \(z\in E\) and some \(b\in\mathbb R\), and let \(\lambda>0\). Then for every \(x\in E\) there is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\). Consequently the proximal map

\[P_\lambda(x)=\text{the unique proximal point of }f\text{ at }x\qquad(x\in E)\]

is well defined, and \(Q_{\lambda,x}(P_\lambda(x))\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\) for all \(x,y\in E\).

Proof. Fix \(x\in E\). Since \(f(x)\ge b\), the number \(s=\sqrt{2\lambda(f(x)-b)}\) is a well-defined nonnegative real, and \(R=s+1>0\).

Continuity. A convex real-valued function on a finite-dimensional real normed space is locally Lipschitz, in particular continuous. The map \(p\mapsto\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\) is continuous as a composition of continuous maps. Hence \(Q_{\lambda,x}\) is continuous.

A minimizer on a ball. In a finite-dimensional normed space closed balls are compact (Heine–Borel). The closed ball \(\bar B=\{p\in E:\|p-x\|\le R\}\) is therefore compact, and it is nonempty because it contains \(x\). A continuous real function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum, so there is \(p\in\bar B\) with \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\) for every \(y\in\bar B\). Taking \(y=x\),

\[Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=f(x).\qquad(1)\]

Competitors outside the ball. Let \(\|y-x\|>R\). Then \(\|y-x\|>s\ge0\), so \(\|y-x\|^2\ge s^2=2\lambda(f(x)-b)\); dividing by \(2\lambda>0\) gives \(f(x)-b\le\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\). Using \(f(y)\ge b\) and then (1),

\[Q_{\lambda,x}(y)=f(y)+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\ge b+\bigl(f(x)-b\bigr)=f(x)\ge Q_{\lambda,x}(p).\]

Together with the minimality on \(\bar B\), this gives \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(y)\) for every \(y\in E\), so \(p\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\).

The proximal map. By the uniqueness proved in the previous step, the proximal point at each input is a single element of \(E\), denoted \(P_\lambda(x)\); by definition it minimizes \(Q_{\lambda,x}\). \(\square\)

The lower bound is used only to make the ball radius finite; convexity is used for continuity, for uniqueness and, through the previous step, for all later properties of \(P_\lambda\).

ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.title: Moreau envelope: gradient, smoothness and uniform approximation
ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) convex and bounded below, \(\lambda>0\), and \(P_\lambda\) the proximal map of the previous section. The Moreau envelope

\[f^\lambda(x)=\min_{p\in E}\Bigl(f(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\Bigr)=f(P_\lambda(x))+\frac{\|P_\lambda(x)-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\]

is shown to be convex and continuously differentiable with gradient \(\nabla f^\lambda(x)=r_\lambda(x)=(x-P_\lambda(x))/\lambda\), and this gradient is \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz. The proof rests on the two-sided bound \(0\le f^\lambda(y)-f^\lambda(x)-\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle\le\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\); no differentiability of \(f\) is assumed.

If moreover \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, then \(\|\nabla f^\lambda\|\le K\), \(\|x-P_\lambda(x)\|\le\lambda K\) and \(0\le f-f^\lambda\le\lambda K^2/2\) on all of \(E\). The gradient formula identifies the smoothed particle algorithms of the later sections with Euler schemes for \(g_1+g_2^\lambda\), and the uniform gap \(\lambda K^2/2\) controls the distance between the smoothed and the original marginal maximizers.

steps.title: The envelope, the residual and two value bounds
steps.body:
Setting. In this section \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is convex and bounded below, and \(\lambda>0\). By the previous section every \(x\in E\) has a unique proximal point \(P_\lambda(x)\), the minimizer of \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\). The Moreau envelope of \(f\) with parameter \(\lambda\) and the proximal residual are

\[f^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}\bigl(P_\lambda(x)\bigr)=\min_{p\in E}Q_{\lambda,x}(p),\qquad r_\lambda(x)=\frac{x-P_\lambda(x)}{\lambda}.\]

Claim. (a) \(f^\lambda(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in E\). (b) If \(b\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(z)\ge b\) for every \(z\in E\), then \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\ge b\) for all \(x,p\in E\); in particular \(f^\lambda(x)\ge b\). Part (b) uses only \(\lambda>0\) and the lower bound.

Proof. (a) \(P_\lambda(x)\) minimizes \(Q_{\lambda,x}\); the competitor \(p=x\) gives \(f^\lambda(x)\le Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=f(x)+0=f(x)\). (b) Since \(\|p-x\|^2\ge0\) and \(2\lambda>0\), \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\ge f(p)\ge b\). Taking \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) gives \(f^\lambda(x)\ge b\). \(\square\)

Thus \(f^\lambda\) is a real-valued function with \(b\le f^\lambda\le f\).

steps.title: Global supports, the quadratic upper bound and convexity
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(x,y\in E\),

\[f^\lambda(x)+\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle\le f^\lambda(y)\le f^\lambda(x)+\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}.\qquad(1)\]

In particular \(r_\lambda(x)\) is a subgradient of \(f^\lambda\) at \(x\), and \(f^\lambda\) is convex.

Proof of the lower bound. Write \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) and \(q=P_\lambda(y)\). By the residual subgradient condition of the previous section (here convexity of \(f\) is used), \(\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p)\). Testing this support at \(q\),

\[f(q)\ge f(p)+\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,q-p\rangle.\qquad(2)\]

Put \(a=q-y\) and \(c=p-x\). Then \(q-p=a-c+(y-x)\) and \(x-p=-c\), so

\[\langle x-p,q-p\rangle=-\langle c,a\rangle+\|c\|^2+\langle x-p,y-x\rangle.\]

Insert this into (2), add \(\|a\|^2/(2\lambda)\) to both sides and subtract \(\|c\|^2/(2\lambda)+\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,y-x\rangle\):

\[f(q)+\frac{\|a\|^2}{2\lambda}-\Bigl(f(p)+\frac{\|c\|^2}{2\lambda}+\frac1\lambda\langle x-p,y-x\rangle\Bigr)\ge\frac{\|a\|^2-2\langle a,c\rangle+\|c\|^2}{2\lambda}=\frac{\|a-c\|^2}{2\lambda}\ge0.\]

Since \(f(q)+\|a\|^2/(2\lambda)=f^\lambda(y)\), \(f(p)+\|c\|^2/(2\lambda)=f^\lambda(x)\) and \(\lambda^{-1}\langle x-p,y-x\rangle=\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle\), this is the lower bound in (1).

Proof of the upper bound. Since \(P_\lambda(y)\) minimizes \(Q_{\lambda,y}\), the competitor \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) gives \(f^\lambda(y)\le Q_{\lambda,y}(p)=f(p)+\|p-y\|^2/(2\lambda)\). Writing \(p-y=(p-x)-(y-x)\),

\[\|p-y\|^2=\|p-x\|^2-2\langle p-x,y-x\rangle+\|y-x\|^2,\]

and therefore

\[Q_{\lambda,y}(p)=f(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}+\frac1\lambda\langle x-p,y-x\rangle+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}=f^\lambda(x)+\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}.\]

This is the upper bound in (1); it uses only the minimality of \(P_\lambda(y)\).

Proof of convexity. Let \(x,y\in E\), \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\), and \(z=ax+by\). The lower bound in (1), based at \(z\) and evaluated at \(x\) and at \(y\), gives

\[f^\lambda(z)+\langle r_\lambda(z),x-z\rangle\le f^\lambda(x),\qquad f^\lambda(z)+\langle r_\lambda(z),y-z\rangle\le f^\lambda(y).\]

Multiply the first inequality by \(a\ge0\), the second by \(b\ge0\), and add. The inner-product terms combine to \(\langle r_\lambda(z),a(x-z)+b(y-z)\rangle\), and \(a(x-z)+b(y-z)=ax+by-(a+b)z=z-z=0\). Since \((a+b)f^\lambda(z)=f^\lambda(z)\), the sum reads \(f^\lambda(ax+by)\le af^\lambda(x)+bf^\lambda(y)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Lipschitz bounds for the proximal map and the residual
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(x,y\in E\),

\[\|P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\|\le\|x-y\|,\qquad\|r_\lambda(x)-r_\lambda(y)\|\le\frac1\lambda\|x-y\|.\]

\[\|r_\lambda(x)-r_\lambda(y)\|=\lambda^{-1}\bigl\|(x-P_\lambda(x))-(y-P_\lambda(y))\bigr\|\le\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|,\]

where the inequality is the nonexpansiveness of the residual map \(x\mapsto x-P_\lambda(x)\) from the previous section. \(\square\)

steps.title: The gradient of the envelope is the scaled residual
steps.body:
Recall that a function \(g:E\to\mathbb R\) has gradient \(v\in E\) at \(x\) if \(g(y)-g(x)-\langle v,y-x\rangle=o(\|y-x\|)\) as \(y\to x\): for every \(c>0\) there is \(\rho>0\) such that

\[|g(y)-g(x)-\langle v,y-x\rangle|\le c\|y-x\|\qquad\text{whenever }\|y-x\|<\rho.\]

Equivalently, \(g\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) with derivative \(h\mapsto\langle v,h\rangle\); \(v\) is then denoted \(\nabla g(x)\).

Claim. For every \(x\in E\), \(f^\lambda\) has gradient \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-P_\lambda(x))\) at \(x\). Consequently \(f^\lambda\) is differentiable on \(E\), \(\nabla f^\lambda=r_\lambda\), and \(f^\lambda\) is continuously differentiable. No differentiability of \(f\) is assumed.

Proof. Fix \(x\) and put \(R(y)=f^\lambda(y)-f^\lambda(x)-\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle\). By (1) of the previous step but one,

\[0\le R(y)\le\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\qquad(y\in E).\qquad(1)\]

Let \(c>0\) and \(\rho=2\lambda c>0\). If \(\|y-x\|<\rho\), then by (1)

\[|R(y)|=R(y)\le\frac{\|y-x\|}{2\lambda}\,\|y-x\|\le\frac{\rho}{2\lambda}\,\|y-x\|=c\,\|y-x\|.\]

Hence \(f^\lambda\) has gradient \(r_\lambda(x)\) at \(x\); in particular it is differentiable at every point and \(\nabla f^\lambda(x)=r_\lambda(x)\).

For the continuity of the derivative, the derivative at \(x\) is the linear functional \(h\mapsto\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\). The map \(v\mapsto\langle v,\cdot\rangle\) from \(E\) to its dual is a linear isometry (Riesz representation), hence continuous, and \(r_\lambda\) is \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz by the previous step, hence continuous. Their composition \(x\mapsto\langle r_\lambda(x),\cdot\rangle\) is continuous. A function that is differentiable everywhere with continuous derivative is continuously differentiable. \(\square\)

By the previous step the gradient \(\nabla f^\lambda\) is \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.

steps.title: Bounded gradient and bounded proximal displacement
steps.body:
Claim. Suppose in addition that \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz for some \(K\ge0\), that is, \(|f(u)-f(v)|\le K\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in E\). Then for every \(x\in E\),

\[\|r_\lambda(x)\|\le K,\qquad\|x-P_\lambda(x)\|\le\lambda K.\]

Proof. Put \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) and \(g=r_\lambda(x)\). By the residual subgradient condition, \(g\in\partial f(p)\). Testing the support inequality at \(y=p+g\) gives \(f(p)+\langle g,g\rangle\le f(p+g)\), so, by the Lipschitz property,

\[\|g\|^2\le f(p+g)-f(p)\le|f(p+g)-f(p)|\le K\|g\|.\]

If \(\|g\|>K\), then \(\|g\|>0\) and \(\|g\|^2>K\|g\|\), contradicting the display; hence \(\|g\|\le K\). Since \(x-P_\lambda(x)=\lambda g\) and \(\lambda>0\), \(\|x-P_\lambda(x)\|=\lambda\|g\|\le\lambda K\). \(\square\)

Because \(\nabla f^\lambda=r_\lambda\), the first inequality bounds the gradient of the envelope by \(K\), uniformly in \(\lambda>0\).

steps.title: The uniform gap between a Lipschitz function and its envelope
steps.body:
Claim. (a) Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be \(K\)-Lipschitz with \(K\ge0\), and \(\lambda>0\). Then for all \(x,p\in E\)

\[Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\ge f(x)-\frac{\lambda K^2}{2};\]

in particular \(f^\lambda(x)\ge f(x)-\lambda K^2/2\). Part (a) uses neither convexity nor a lower bound. (b) If \(f\) is in addition convex and bounded below, then for every \(x\in E\)

\[0\le f(x)-f^\lambda(x)\le\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}.\]

Proof. (a) Let \(d=\|p-x\|\). The Lipschitz property gives \(f(x)-f(p)\le|f(x)-f(p)|\le Kd\), i.e. \(f(p)\ge f(x)-Kd\). Completing the square in \(d\),

\[\frac{d^2}{2\lambda}-Kd=\frac{(d-\lambda K)^2}{2\lambda}-\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}\ge-\frac{\lambda K^2}{2},\]

because \((d-\lambda K)^2\ge0\) and \(2\lambda>0\). Hence \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\ge f(x)-Kd+d^2/(2\lambda)\ge f(x)-\lambda K^2/2\).

(b) The inequality \(f(x)-f^\lambda(x)\ge0\) is part (a) of the first step, and \(f(x)-f^\lambda(x)\le\lambda K^2/2\) is part (a) of this step with \(p=P_\lambda(x)\). \(\square\)

The gap is uniform in \(x\) and linear in \(\lambda\). For any function \(g_1\), writing \(U=g_1+f\) and \(V_\lambda=g_1+f^\lambda\), it gives \(V_\lambda\le U\le V_\lambda+\lambda K^2/2\) on all of \(E\); this two-sided comparison is the form in which the gap enters the comparison of marginal potentials.

ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.title: Strong convexity of the Moreau envelope of a strongly convex function
ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(m\ge0\), \(\lambda>0\), and let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below. This section proves that the Moreau envelope \(f^\lambda(x)=\min_p\bigl(f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\bigr)\) is \(m/(1+m\lambda)\)-strongly convex. The proof tests the minimization that defines \(f^\lambda(ax+by)\) with the convex combination \(aP_\lambda(x)+bP_\lambda(y)\) of the two proximal points, and combines the strong-convexity deficit of \(f\) with the deficit of the quadratic penalty by completing a square. Differentiability of \(f\) is not used.

The result is used when the whole strongly convex potential is smoothed, as in PIPULA. When only a convex summand \(g_2\) is smoothed and an \(m\)-strongly convex \(g_1\) is kept, the sum \(g_1+g_2^\lambda\) keeps the modulus \(m\), because \(g_2^\lambda\) is convex.

steps.title: Two quadratic identities
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real inner-product space and \(u,v\in E\).

  1. If \(a,b\ge0\) and \(a+b=1\), then \[\|au+bv\|^2=a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2-ab\|u-v\|^2.\qquad(1)\]
  2. If \(m\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\), then \[\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|v\|^2\le m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}.\qquad(2)\]

Proof. (a) Expanding the squared norms by bilinearity of the inner product,

\[\|au+bv\|^2=a^2\|u\|^2+2ab\langle u,v\rangle+b^2\|v\|^2,\qquad ab\|u-v\|^2=ab\|u\|^2-2ab\langle u,v\rangle+ab\|v\|^2.\]

Hence \(a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2-ab\|u-v\|^2=a(1-b)\|u\|^2+2ab\langle u,v\rangle+b(1-a)\|v\|^2\), and since \(1-b=a\) and \(1-a=b\), this equals \(\|au+bv\|^2\).

(b) Put \(c=1+m\lambda\). Since \(m\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\), \(c\ge1>0\). We show

\[m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}-\frac{m}{c}\|v\|^2=\frac{\|cu-v\|^2}{\lambda c}.\qquad(3)\]

Multiply the left side by \(\lambda c>0\) and expand \(\|u-v\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\):

\[\begin{aligned} m\lambda c\|u\|^2+c\bigl(\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\bigr)-m\lambda\|v\|^2 &=c(1+m\lambda)\|u\|^2-2c\langle u,v\rangle+(c-m\lambda)\|v\|^2\\ &=c^2\|u\|^2-2c\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2=\|cu-v\|^2 . \end{aligned}\]

Dividing by \(\lambda c\) gives (3). The right-hand side of (3) is nonnegative, because it is a square divided by the positive number \(\lambda c\); this is (2). \(\square\)

For \(v=cu\) the right-hand side of (3) vanishes, so equality holds in (2) and the constant \(m/(1+m\lambda)\) cannot be replaced by a larger one.

steps.title: The envelope of an \(m\)-strongly convex function is \(m/(1+m\lambda)\)-strongly convex
steps.body:
Recall that \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is \(m\)-strongly convex if for all \(x,y\in E\) and all \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\),

\[f(ax+by)\le af(x)+bf(y)-ab\,\frac m2\,\|x-y\|^2.\]

For \(m=0\) this is convexity; for \(m\ge0\) an \(m\)-strongly convex function is convex.

Claim. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, \(m\ge0\), \(\lambda>0\), and let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below. Then \(f^\lambda\) is \(m_\lambda\)-strongly convex, where

\[m_\lambda=\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}.\]

Proof. Since \(m\ge0\), \(f\) is convex; together with the lower bound and finite dimension this gives the proximal map \(P_\lambda\) and the envelope \(f^\lambda\) of the previous sections. Let \(x,y\in E\), \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\), and put \(z=ax+by\), \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), \(q=P_\lambda(y)\). Since \(P_\lambda(z)\) minimizes \(Q_{\lambda,z}\), the competitor \(ap+bq\) gives

\[f^\lambda(z)\le f(ap+bq)+\frac{\|ap+bq-z\|^2}{2\lambda}.\qquad(4)\]

Since \(ap+bq-z=a(p-x)+b(q-y)\), identity (1) of the previous step with \(u=p-x\) and \(v=q-y\), for which \(u-v=(p-q)-(x-y)\), gives

\[\|ap+bq-z\|^2=a\|p-x\|^2+b\|q-y\|^2-ab\,\|(p-q)-(x-y)\|^2.\]

Strong convexity of \(f\) at \(p,q\) gives \(f(ap+bq)\le af(p)+bf(q)-ab\frac m2\|p-q\|^2\). Inserting both into (4) and regrouping,

\[f^\lambda(z)\le a\Bigl(f(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda}\Bigr)+b\Bigl(f(q)+\frac{\|q-y\|^2}{2\lambda}\Bigr)-\frac{ab}{2}\Bigl(m\|p-q\|^2+\frac{\|(p-q)-(x-y)\|^2}{\lambda}\Bigr).\]

The first two brackets are \(f^\lambda(x)\) and \(f^\lambda(y)\). By (2) of the previous step with \(u=p-q\) and \(v=x-y\), the last bracket is at least \(m_\lambda\|x-y\|^2\); since \(ab\ge0\), the last term is at most \(-\frac{ab}{2}m_\lambda\|x-y\|^2\). Therefore

\[f^\lambda(ax+by)\le af^\lambda(x)+bf^\lambda(y)-ab\,\frac{m_\lambda}{2}\,\|x-y\|^2 .\]

This is \(m_\lambda\)-strong convexity of \(f^\lambda\). \(\square\)

No derivative of \(f\) appears in the argument. For \(m=0\) the claim reduces to convexity of the envelope.

ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.title: A distance–energy inequality for one proximal step
ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real inner-product space, \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) convex, \(\eta>0\) and \(x\in E\), and let \(p\) be a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) with parameter \(\eta\), i.e. a global minimizer of \(f(\cdot)+\|\cdot-x\|^2/(2\eta)\). If \(s\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at the input point \(x\), then for every comparison point \(a\in E\)

\[\|p-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta\bigl(f(x)-f(a)\bigr)+\eta^2\|s\|^2.\]

Thus one proximal step decreases the squared distance to any point \(a\) by \(2\eta\) times the energy excess \(f(x)-f(a)\), up to the error \(\eta^2\|s\|^2\). This is the deterministic inequality used in Lemma A.8 of Cordero Encinar, Crucinio and Akyildiz (arXiv:2406.14292v3); a bound \(\|s\|^2\le C\) turns the error into \(\eta^2C\). Any subgradient at \(x\) may be used. The inequality is applied pairwise to the particle updates in the next section and, with a random comparison point, in the energy estimate of the splitting scheme.

steps.title: The energy inequality for an arbitrary proximal point
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be convex, \(\eta>0\), \(x,p,s,a\in E\). Assume that \(p\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) with parameter \(\eta\) and that \(s\in\partial f(x)\), i.e. \(f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in E\). Then

\[\|p-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta\bigl(f(x)-f(a)\bigr)+\eta^2\|s\|^2.\]

Proof. Put \(d=x-p\). Four facts are combined.

Support at the output. Since \(f\) is convex and \(p\) is a proximal point, the residual \(\eta^{-1}d\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(p\). Testing it at \(a\) gives \(f(p)+\eta^{-1}\langle d,a-p\rangle\le f(a)\); multiplying by \(\eta>0\) and using \(a-p=-(p-a)\),

\[\eta f(p)-\langle d,p-a\rangle\le\eta f(a).\qquad(1)\]

Support at the input. Testing \(s\in\partial f(x)\) at \(y=p\) and using \(p-x=-d\),

\[f(x)-\langle s,d\rangle\le f(p).\qquad(2)\]

Expansion of the distance. Since \(x-a=d+(p-a)\),

\[\|x-a\|^2=\|d\|^2+2\langle d,p-a\rangle+\|p-a\|^2.\qquad(3)\]

A completed square. Expanding \(\|d-\eta s\|^2\ge0\),

\[2\eta\langle s,d\rangle-\|d\|^2\le\eta^2\|s\|^2.\qquad(4)\]

Now, by (3), then (1) multiplied by \(2\), then (2) multiplied by \(2\eta>0\), and finally (4),

\[\begin{aligned} \|p-a\|^2&=\|x-a\|^2-\|d\|^2-2\langle d,p-a\rangle\\ &\le\|x-a\|^2-\|d\|^2+2\eta\bigl(f(a)-f(p)\bigr)\\ &\le\|x-a\|^2-\|d\|^2+2\eta\bigl(f(a)-f(x)\bigr)+2\eta\langle s,d\rangle\\ &\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta\bigl(f(x)-f(a)\bigr)+\eta^2\|s\|^2. \qquad\square \end{aligned}\]

Convexity enters only through the residual subgradient (1), and the subgradient \(s\) at the input only through (2) and (4). The point \(a\) is arbitrary and need not be related to \(x\) or \(p\).

steps.title: The inequality for the proximal map and under a subgradient bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) convex and bounded below, \(\eta>0\), \(x,s,a\in E\) with \(s\in\partial f(x)\), and let \(P_\eta\) be the proximal map of \(f\) with parameter \(\eta\). Then

\[\|P_\eta(x)-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta\bigl(f(x)-f(a)\bigr)+\eta^2\|s\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

If moreover \(\|s\|^2\le C\) for a real number \(C\), then

\[\|P_\eta(x)-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta\bigl(f(x)-f(a)\bigr)+\eta^2C.\qquad(2)\]

Proof. Under these hypotheses \(P_\eta(x)\) is a proximal point of \(f\) at \(x\) (existence of proximal points), so (1) is the previous step with \(p=P_\eta(x)\). Since \(\eta^2\ge0\), \(\|s\|^2\le C\) implies \(\eta^2\|s\|^2\le\eta^2C\), and (2) follows from (1). \(\square\)

A numerical bound on \(\|s\|^2\) controls only the last term; \(s\) must still be a subgradient at \(x\). For a convex \(K\)-Lipschitz function every subgradient satisfies \(\|s\|\le K\), so (2) holds with \(C=K^2\).

ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.title: The energy inequality for averaged pairwise proximal outputs
ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.summary:
Fix \(N\ge1\) particles and dimensions \(d_\theta,d_x\). The pair space is \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), and the state space is \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) with points \(z=(\theta,z_1,\dots,z_N)\), Euclidean norm \(\|z\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\sum_i\|z_i\|^2\), and physical particles \(x_i=\sqrt N z_i\). The \(i\)-th pair of a state is \(J_iz=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), and the lifted potential of a pair function \(g\) is \(F_g(z)=\sum_{i=1}^Ng(J_iz)\). Given any map \(P\) of the pair space, the pairwise map \(\mathcal P\) applies \(P\) to each pair, averages the \(N\) parameter outputs and rescales the latent outputs:

\[(\mathcal Pz)_\theta=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_\theta,\qquad(\mathcal Pz)_i=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_x .\]

This section proves \(\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|P(J_iz)-J_ia\|^2\) for every \(P\) (Jensen's inequality for the averaged parameter, exact scaling for the latent blocks), and combines it with the single-pair energy inequality of the previous section. For \(P=P_\lambda\), the proximal map of a convex, bounded-below pair function \(g\) with bounded subgradients, the result is

\[\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\le\|z-a\|^2-\frac{2\lambda}{N}\bigl(F_g(z)-F_g(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C.\]

The averaged output is in general not a proximal point of \(F_g\) on the state space, so this inequality is proved directly; it is the deterministic energy estimate used for the PIPGLA splitting scheme.

steps.title: Jensen's inequality for the averaged parameter
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\).

  1. For real numbers \(b_1,\dots,b_N\), \[N\Bigl(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i\Bigr)^2\le\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i^2.\qquad(1)\]
  2. For every map \(P\) from the pair space to itself and all states \(z,a\), \[\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\le\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl\|P(J_iz)-J_ia\bigr\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

Proof. (a) By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in \(\mathbb R^N\) applied to \((1,\dots,1)\) and \((b_1,\dots,b_N)\), \(\bigl(\sum_ib_i\bigr)^2\le N\sum_ib_i^2\). Dividing by \(N>0\) gives \(N\bigl(N^{-1}\sum_ib_i\bigr)^2=N^{-1}\bigl(\sum_ib_i\bigr)^2\le\sum_ib_i^2\).

(b) Write \(p_i=P(J_iz)=(p_{i,\theta},p_{i,x})\) and \(a=(a_\theta,a_1,\dots,a_N)\), so that \(J_ia=(a_\theta,\sqrt Na_i)\). By the definition of the Euclidean norm on the state space,

\[N\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2=N\Bigl\|\frac1N\sum_ip_{i,\theta}-a_\theta\Bigr\|^2+\sum_{i=1}^NN\Bigl\|\frac{1}{\sqrt N}p_{i,x}-a_i\Bigr\|^2.\qquad(3)\]

Parameter block. For each parameter coordinate \(j\), the common comparison value can be moved inside the average: \(N^{-1}\sum_ip_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}=N^{-1}\sum_i(p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j})\). By (1) with \(b_i=p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\),

\[N\Bigl(\frac1N\sum_ip_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\Bigr)^2\le\sum_i\bigl(p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\bigr)^2 .\]

Summing over \(j\) gives \(N\|N^{-1}\sum_ip_{i,\theta}-a_\theta\|^2\le\sum_i\|p_{i,\theta}-a_\theta\|^2\).

Latent blocks. For each \(i\) and each latent coordinate \(j\), \(\sqrt N\bigl(N^{-1/2}p_{i,x,j}-a_{i,j}\bigr)=p_{i,x,j}-\sqrt Na_{i,j}\); squaring and using \((\sqrt N)^2=N\),

\[N\bigl(N^{-1/2}p_{i,x,j}-a_{i,j}\bigr)^2=\bigl(p_{i,x,j}-\sqrt Na_{i,j}\bigr)^2 .\]

Summing over \(j\) gives \(N\|N^{-1/2}p_{i,x}-a_i\|^2=\|p_{i,x}-\sqrt Na_i\|^2\), an equality.

Inserting both into (3),

\[N\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^N\Bigl(\|p_{i,\theta}-a_\theta\|^2+\|p_{i,x}-\sqrt Na_i\|^2\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^N\|p_i-J_ia\|^2,\]

and dividing by \(N>0\) gives (2). \(\square\)

Only (1) is an inequality; the latent contributions are equalities. No property of \(P\) is used.

steps.title: Summing the pairwise proximal energy inequalities
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), let \(g\) be a convex function on the pair space that is bounded below, let \(\lambda>0\), let \(z,a\) be states and \(C\in\mathbb R\). Assume that for every \(i\) there is a subgradient \(s_i\) of \(g\) at \(J_iz\) with \(\|s_i\|^2\le C\). Let \(\mathcal P\) be the pairwise map built from the proximal map \(P_\lambda\) of \(g\). Then

\[\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\le\|z-a\|^2-\frac{2\lambda}{N}\bigl(F_g(z)-F_g(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C .\]

Proof. Pairwise inequalities. For each \(i\), the energy inequality of the previous section (convexity and lower bound of \(g\), \(\lambda>0\), subgradient \(s_i\) at the input \(J_iz\) with \(\|s_i\|^2\le C\), comparison point \(J_ia\)) gives

\[\|P_\lambda(J_iz)-J_ia\|^2\le\|J_iz-J_ia\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(g(J_iz)-g(J_ia)\bigr)+\lambda^2C.\qquad(1)\]

The norm identity. Each \(J_i\) is linear, so \(J_iz-J_ia=J_i(z-a)\). For any state \(w=(w_\theta,w_1,\dots,w_N)\),

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_iw\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(\|w_\theta\|^2+N\|w_i\|^2\bigr)=N\|w_\theta\|^2+N\sum_{i=1}^N\|w_i\|^2=N\|w\|^2,\qquad(2)\]

because the parameter block occurs in each of the \(N\) pairs and each latent block occurs in one pair, multiplied by \(\sqrt N\).

Summation. Summing (1) over \(i\) and using (2) with \(w=z-a\) and \(\sum_ig(J_iz)=F_g(z)\),

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|P_\lambda(J_iz)-J_ia\|^2\le N\|z-a\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(F_g(z)-F_g(a)\bigr)+N\lambda^2C .\]

By (2) of the previous step applied to \(P=P_\lambda\), the left-hand side divided by \(N\) bounds \(\|\mathcal Pz-a\|^2\). Dividing the display by \(N>0\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

The minimizing property of \(P_\lambda\) is used only pair by pair, in (1). The averaged output \(\mathcal Pz\) is not, in general, a minimizer of \(w\mapsto F_g(w)+N\|w-z\|^2/(2\lambda)\) on the state space; an explicit two-particle example is given in . The inequality of this step is therefore proved for the averaged map itself. A subgradient of minimal norm, when available, is one admissible choice of \(s_i\).

ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.title: The update maps of MYIPLA, PIPULA and PIPGLA
ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.summary:
This section defines the three proximal interacting particle algorithms as deterministic maps of a state and an innovation, and proves the algebraic identities relating them. The state space is \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) with scaled coordinates \(z=(\theta,z_1,\dots,z_N)\) (physical particles \(x_i=\sqrt Nz_i\)), \(J_iz=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\) is the \(i\)-th parameter–particle pair, and \(F_g(z)=\sum_{i=1}^Ng(J_iz)\) is the lifted potential of a pair function \(g\). For a map \(P\) of the pair space, \(\mathcal P\) denotes the pairwise map that applies \(P\) to every pair, averages the parameter outputs and divides the latent outputs by \(\sqrt N\). With step \(\gamma\), smoothing parameter \(\eta\) and innovation \(\xi\) in the state space:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{PIPULA:}\quad&z\mapsto\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi,\\ \text{MYIPLA:}\quad&z\mapsto\Bigl(1-\frac\gamma\eta\Bigr)z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\frac\gamma\eta\,\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi,\\ \text{PIPGLA:}\quad&z\mapsto\mathcal P\Bigl(z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi\Bigr). \end{aligned}\]

Each algorithm is the recursion \(Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\) driven by a given innovation sequence. We prove that PIPULA is MYIPLA with \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\), write MYIPLA in parameter and physical-particle coordinates, and prove that if \(\nabla e=\eta^{-1}(I-P)\) (as for \(e=g_2^\eta\) and \(P=P_\eta\)) then MYIPLA coincides, iterate by iterate, with the Euler scheme (IPLA) for the smooth potential \(g_1+e\). PIPGLA applies the proximal map after the noisy gradient step and has no such identity; it is analysed separately. No probabilistic assumption enters this section.

steps.title: The pairwise map in coordinates
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(P\) be any map from the pair space \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\) to itself, and write \(P(w)=([P(w)]_\theta,[P(w)]_x)\). The pairwise map \(\mathcal P\) on the state space is defined by

\[(\mathcal Pz)_\theta=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_\theta,\qquad(\mathcal Pz)_i=\frac1{\sqrt N}\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_x\quad(i=1,\dots,N).\]

Claim. For every parameter coordinate \(j\le d_\theta\), every particle \(i\) and every latent coordinate \(j\le d_x\), the coordinates of \(\mathcal Pz\) are \(N^{-1}\sum_i[P(J_iz)]_{\theta,j}\) and \(N^{-1/2}[P(J_iz)]_{x,j}\).

Proof. This is the definition read coordinatewise. \(\square\)

All \(N\) pairs are formed with the same current parameter \(\theta\). The \(N\) proposed parameters \([P(J_iz)]_\theta\) are averaged into one new parameter, while the latent output of pair \(i\) is a physical particle and is divided by \(\sqrt N\) to return to scaled coordinates. When \(P\) is a proximal map, \(\mathcal P\) need not be the proximal map of any function on the state space.

steps.title: The PIPULA, MYIPLA and PIPGLA update maps
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(P\) be a map of the pair space, \(g_1\) a real function on the pair space, \(\gamma,\eta\in\mathbb R\), and \(z,\xi\) states. The gradient of the lifted potential \(F_{g_1}(z)=\sum_ig_1(J_iz)\) is taken on the state space with its Euclidean inner product. The three update maps are

\[\begin{aligned} T_{\mathrm{PIPULA}}(z,\xi)&=\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi,\\ T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)&=\Bigl(1-\frac\gamma\eta\Bigr)z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\frac\gamma\eta\,\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi,\\ T_{\mathrm{PIPGLA}}(z,\xi)&=\mathcal P\bigl(S_\gamma(z,\xi)\bigr),\qquad S_\gamma(z,\xi)=z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi . \end{aligned}\]

\(S_\gamma\) is the scaled Euler (IPLA) step for the potential \(g_1\) with step \(\gamma\). In PIPULA the proximal pairwise map is applied to the current state and the Gaussian increment is added afterwards. In MYIPLA the proximal output enters through the term \(\frac\gamma\eta(\mathcal Pz-z)\), which for \(P=P_\eta\) is \(-\gamma\) times the scaled Moreau residual (see the last step), and \(\eta\) and \(\gamma\) are independent. In PIPGLA the proximal pairwise map is applied after the noisy gradient step, so the increment passes through \(\mathcal P\). For the same input the three maps generally give different outputs, and their analyses are separate.

The definitions involve no hypothesis on \(P\), \(g_1\), \(\gamma\) or \(\eta\); the results that use them assume \(\gamma>0\) (and \(\eta>0\) for MYIPLA) wherever the noise coefficient or the ratio \(\gamma/\eta\) matters.

steps.title: Recursions driven by an innovation sequence
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(X\) be a set, \(T:X\times X\to X\) an update map, \(z_0\in X\) and \((\xi_n)_{n\ge0}\) a sequence in \(X\). The chain driven by \((\xi_n)\) is the sequence defined recursively by

\[Z_0=z_0,\qquad Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\quad(n\ge0).\]

By the recursion theorem this defines a unique sequence. The MYIPLA, PIPULA and PIPGLA chains are the chains of \(T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{PIPULA}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{PIPGLA}}\) on the state space.

Claim. \(Z_0=z_0\) and \(Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\) for every \(n\).

Proof. These are the two defining equations. \(\square\)

The definition is deterministic: the innovations are arbitrary elements of the state space, and no distribution, independence or measurability is assumed. When the initial state and the innovations are random variables, the \(n\)-th iterate is the composition of \(n\) applications of \(T\) with these inputs, and its law is determined by the joint law of \((z_0,\xi_0,\dots,\xi_{n-1})\) once \(T\) is measurable; these probabilistic statements are proved in later sections.

steps.title: PIPULA is MYIPLA without smooth part and with equal scales
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a map of the pair space and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\).

  1. For every state \(z\), innovation \(\xi\) and parameter coordinate \(j\), \[T_{\mathrm{PIPULA}}(z,\xi)_{\theta,j}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_{\theta,j}+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi_{\theta,j}.\]
  2. If \(\gamma\ne0\), then \(T_{\mathrm{PIPULA}}(z,\xi)=T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)\) for all \(z,\xi\), where \(T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}\) is formed with \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\).
  3. If \(\gamma\ne0\), the PIPULA chain and the MYIPLA chain with \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\), started at the same \(z_0\) and driven by the same innovations, coincide: \(Z_n^{\mathrm{PIPULA}}=Z_n^{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}\) for every \(n\).

Proof. (a) is the parameter coordinate of \(\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi\) given by the previous coordinate formula.

(b) With \(g_1=0\) the lifted potential \(F_{g_1}\) is identically \(0\), so its gradient vanishes. With \(\eta=\gamma\ne0\), \(1-\gamma/\eta=0\) and \(\gamma/\eta=1\). Hence \(T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)=0\cdot z-0+1\cdot\mathcal Pz+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi=T_{\mathrm{PIPULA}}(z,\xi)\).

(c) By (b) the two update maps are equal as functions, so the two recursions with the same initial value and the same innovations define the same sequence; formally, induction on \(n\) with base case \(Z_0=z_0\) for both chains and inductive step \(Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\) with the common map \(T\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(\gamma\ne0\) is needed for \(\gamma/\gamma=1\).

Claim. Let \(g_1\) be differentiable, \(P\) a map of the pair space, \(\eta,\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and \(z,\xi\) states; write \(z^+=T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)\).

  1. For every parameter coordinate \(j\), \[z^+_{\theta,j}=\Bigl(1-\frac\gamma\eta\Bigr)\theta_j-\frac\gamma N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_j}g_1(J_iz)+\frac\gamma\eta\cdot\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_{\theta,j}+\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi_{\theta,j}.\]
  2. If \(N\ge1\), then for every particle \(i\) and latent coordinate \(j\), with \(x_{i,j}=\sqrt Nz_{i,j}\) and \(x^+_{i,j}=\sqrt Nz^+_{i,j}\), \[x^+_{i,j}=\Bigl(1-\frac\gamma\eta\Bigr)x_{i,j}-\gamma\,\partial_{x_j}g_1(J_iz)+\frac\gamma\eta\bigl[P(J_iz)\bigr]_{x,j}+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_{i,j}.\]

Proof. (a) Take the parameter coordinate of each term of \(T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}\): the first gives \((1-\gamma/\eta)\theta_j\), the second gives \(-(\gamma/N)\sum_i\partial_{\theta_j}g_1(J_iz)\) by the parameter block formula, the third is \(\gamma/\eta\) times the parameter coordinate of \(\mathcal Pz\), and the fourth is \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi_{\theta,j}\).

(b) Take the \((i,j)\) latent coordinate of each term and multiply by \(\sqrt N\). The first term gives \((1-\gamma/\eta)\sqrt Nz_{i,j}\). By the latent block formula the second gives \(-\frac\gamma N\sqrt N\cdot\sqrt N\,\partial_{x_j}g_1(J_iz)=-\gamma\,\partial_{x_j}g_1(J_iz)\), since \((\sqrt N)^2=N\) and \(N\ne0\). The third gives \(\frac\gamma\eta\sqrt N\cdot N^{-1/2}[P(J_iz)]_{x,j}=\frac\gamma\eta[P(J_iz)]_{x,j}\), since \(\sqrt N\ne0\). The fourth gives \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi_{i,j}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_{i,j}\), because \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}=\sqrt{N\cdot2\gamma/N}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\) (the product rule \(\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}\) for \(a\ge0\)). \(\square\)

In physical coordinates, the parameter moves by the average force \(N^{-1}\sum_i\nabla_\theta g_1\) times \(\gamma\) with noise of variance \(2\gamma/N\) per coordinate, while each particle moves by its own force times \(\gamma\) with noise of variance \(2\gamma\) per coordinate.

steps.title: MYIPLA is the Euler scheme for the smoothed potential
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), let \(e\) be a differentiable function on the pair space, \(P\) a map of the pair space and \(\eta e0\) such that

\[ abla e(w)=\eta^{-1} igl(w-P(w) igr)\qquad ext{for every pair }w.\qquad(1)\]
  1. For every state \(z\), \(\mathcal Pz=z- rac\eta N abla F_e(z)\).
  2. In a complete real inner-product space, if \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable then \( abla(f+g)(x)= abla f(x)+ abla g(x)\).
  3. If moreover \(g_1\) is differentiable, then for all \(\gamma\) and all states \(z,\xi\), \[T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)=z- rac\gamma N abla F_{g_1+e}(z)+\sqrt{ rac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi,\] the scaled Euler step for the potential \(g_1+e\).
  4. Under the same hypotheses the MYIPLA chain coincides with the scaled Euler chain for \(g_1+e\) with step \(\gamma\), started at the same \(z_0\) with the same innovations, at every iteration \(n\).

The main application is \(e=g_2^\eta\) and \(P=P_\eta\) for a convex, bounded-below \(g_2\) and \(\eta>0\): then (1) is the Moreau gradient formula, and MYIPLA is the Euler scheme for \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\).

Proof. (a) By (1), \(P(w)=w-\eta abla e(w)\). Parameter block: using \([J_iz]_ heta= heta\) and the parameter block formula of the previous step,

\[(\mathcal Pz)_ heta= rac1N\sum_{i=1}^N igl( heta-\eta abla_ heta e(J_iz) igr)= heta- rac\eta N\sum_{i=1}^N abla_ heta e(J_iz)= heta- rac\eta N abla_ heta F_e(z).\]

Latent block \(i\): using \([J_iz]_x=\sqrt Nz_i\) and the latent block formula,

\[(\mathcal Pz)_i= rac1{\sqrt N} igl(\sqrt Nz_i-\eta abla_xe(J_iz) igr)=z_i- rac{\eta}{\sqrt N} abla_xe(J_iz)=z_i- rac\eta N\sqrt N\, abla_xe(J_iz)=z_i- rac\eta N abla_{z_i}F_e(z),\]

where \(1/\sqrt N=\sqrt N/N\) because \((\sqrt N)^2=N>0\).

(b) The Fréchet derivative of a sum of two functions differentiable at \(x\) is the sum of the derivatives, and the vector representing a functional depends linearly on the functional.

(c) The lifted potential is additive: \(F_{g_1+e}(z)=\sum_i igl(g_1(J_iz)+e(J_iz) igr)=F_{g_1}(z)+F_e(z)\), and both summands are differentiable (compositions of differentiable functions with the linear maps \(J_i\)), so by (b) \( abla F_{g_1+e}= abla F_{g_1}+ abla F_e\). Substituting (a) into the definition of \(T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}\),

\[ egin{aligned} T_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(z,\xi)&=\Bigl(1- rac\gamma\eta\Bigr)z- rac\gamma N abla F_{g_1}(z)+ rac\gamma\eta\Bigl(z- rac\eta N abla F_e(z)\Bigr)+\sqrt{ rac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi\ &=z- rac\gamma N igl( abla F_{g_1}(z)+ abla F_e(z) igr)+\sqrt{ rac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi=z- rac\gamma N abla F_{g_1+e}(z)+\sqrt{ rac{2\gamma}N}\,\xi, \end{aligned}\]

where \( rac\gamma\eta\cdot rac\eta N= rac\gamma N\) uses \(\eta e0\).

(d) Induction on \(n\). Both chains equal \(z_0\) at \(n=0\). If they agree at \(n\), then at \(n+1\) both are obtained by applying the respective update to the same state and the same innovation \(\xi_n\), and these updates agree by (c). \(\square\)

ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.title: MYIPLA: laws, moments and the error bound about the smoothed marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.summary:
Let \(g_1\) be a differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex pair potential with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(g_2\) be convex and bounded below, and let \(\eta>0\). The smoothed pair potential is \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), where \(g_2^\eta\) is the Moreau envelope, and \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\). By the previous sections \(V_\eta\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \(\nabla V_\eta\) is \(L_\eta\)-Lipschitz, and MYIPLA with the proximal map \(P_\eta\) of \(g_2\) is, iterate by iterate, the IPLA scheme for \(V_\eta\). This section turns these identities into statements about the laws \(\rho_n\) of the MYIPLA iterates on a probability space \((\Omega,Q)\).

We prove: \(\rho_n\) is the law of the IPLA iterate for \(V_\eta\); \(\rho_n\) is a probability measure whose parameter block has finite second moment for every \(L^2\) initialization and \(L^2\) innovations; and, for independent standard Gaussian innovations independent of the initialization and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\),

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta^\star_\eta\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V_\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\,\sqrt\gamma,\]

where \(\theta_n\) is the parameter block of the \(n\)-th iterate, \(\theta^\star_\eta\) a maximizer of the smoothed marginal likelihood \(\theta\mapsto\int e^{-V_\eta(\theta,x)}\,dx\) and \(\pi_{N,V_\eta}\) the Gibbs target of the smoothed model. The next section replaces \(\theta^\star_\eta\) by the maximizer of the original nonsmooth model.

steps.title: Curvature and gradient regularity of the smoothed potential
steps.body:
Definitions. For pair potentials \(g_1,g_2\) and \(\eta>0\), the smoothed potential is \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), and for \(L_1\ge0\) the smoothed gradient constant is \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\).

Claim. Let \(E\) be a real normed space (in (b), a complete real inner-product space).

  1. If \(g_1:E\to\mathbb R\) is \(m\)-strongly convex and \(e:E\to\mathbb R\) is convex, then \(g_1+e\) is \(m\)-strongly convex.
  2. If \(g_1\) and \(e\) are differentiable, \(\nabla g_1\) is \(L_1\)-Lipschitz and \(\nabla e\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz, then \(\nabla(g_1+e)\) is \((L_1+L_2)\)-Lipschitz.

In particular, if \(g_1\) is differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g_2\) is convex and bounded below on a finite-dimensional space, then \(V_\eta\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_\eta\)-Lipschitz gradient.

Proof. (a) Let \(x,y\in E\), \(a,b\ge0\), \(a+b=1\). Strong convexity of \(g_1\) and convexity of \(e\) give

\[g_1(ax+by)\le ag_1(x)+bg_1(y)-ab\frac m2\|x-y\|^2,\qquad e(ax+by)\le ae(x)+be(y).\]

Adding the two inequalities gives the \(m\)-strong convexity inequality for \(g_1+e\).

(b) By additivity of the gradient of differentiable functions (previous section), \(\nabla(g_1+e)=\nabla g_1+\nabla e\). By the triangle inequality,

\[\|\nabla(g_1+e)(x)-\nabla(g_1+e)(y)\|\le\|\nabla g_1(x)-\nabla g_1(y)\|+\|\nabla e(x)-\nabla e(y)\|\le(L_1+L_2)\|x-y\|.\]

For the final statement apply (a) and (b) with \(e=g_2^\eta\), which is convex and differentiable with \(\eta^{-1}\)-Lipschitz gradient by the Moreau envelope section, so \(L_2=\eta^{-1}\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The MYIPLA laws are IPLA laws and have finite second moments
steps.body:
Setting. Let \((\Omega,Q)\) be a probability space, \(Z_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) an initial state and \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) innovations, all square-integrable random vectors. For \(\omega\in\Omega\) let \(Z_n(\omega)\) be the MYIPLA chain started at \(Z_0(\omega)\) and driven by \((\xi_k(\omega))_k\). The law of the \(n\)-th iterate is the pushforward measure \(\rho_n=Q\circ Z_n^{-1}\), \(\rho_n(A)=Q(Z_n\in A)\). Write \(\theta(z)\) for the parameter block of a state \(z\).

Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), let \(g_1,e\) be differentiable pair functions, \(P\) a map of the pair space and \(\eta\ne0\) with \(\nabla e=\eta^{-1}(I-P)\). Let \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and assume that \(\nabla(g_1+e)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Then for every \(n\):

  1. \(\rho_n\) equals the law of the \(n\)-th IPLA iterate for the potential \(g_1+e\) with step \(\gamma\), started at \(Z_0\) and driven by the same innovations;
  2. for every \(\vartheta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\), \(\int\|\theta(z)-\vartheta\|^2\,\rho_n(dz)<\infty\).

Proof. (a) By the last identity of the previous section, \(Z_n(\omega)\) coincides for every \(\omega\) with the IPLA iterate \(Y_n(\omega)\) for \(g_1+e\) driven by the same inputs. Equal maps have equal pushforwards, so \(\rho_n=Q\circ Y_n^{-1}\).

(b) Since \(\nabla(g_1+e)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, the lifted gradient \(\nabla F_{g_1+e}\) is Lipschitz on the state space, hence of at most linear growth: \(\|\nabla F_{g_1+e}(z)\|\le\|\nabla F_{g_1+e}(0)\|+NL\|z\|\). The IPLA step \(z\mapsto z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1+e}(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\xi\) therefore maps square-integrable random vectors to square-integrable random vectors, and by induction on \(n\) the iterate \(Y_n\) is square-integrable (and measurable). The parameter projection \(z\mapsto\theta(z)\) is linear with norm at most \(1\), so \(\theta(Y_n)-\vartheta\) is square-integrable on the probability space \((\Omega,Q)\), constants being square-integrable there. By the change-of-variables formula for pushforward measures,

\[\int\|\theta(z)-\vartheta\|^2\,\rho_n(dz)=\int_\Omega\|\theta(Y_n(\omega))-\vartheta\|^2\,Q(d\omega)<\infty .\ \square\]

No Gaussianity, independence or convexity is used here; only the Lipschitz gradient and the square-integrability of the inputs.

steps.title: The error bound for a general smoothing with residual gradient
steps.body:
Definitions. The Gibbs target of a pair potential \(V\) is the probability measure on the state space with density proportional to \(e^{-F_V(z)}\), \(F_V(z)=\sum_iV(J_iz)\); it is denoted \(\pi_{N,V}\). A marginal maximizer of \(V\) is a point \(\theta^\star\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(k_V(\theta)\le k_V(\theta^\star)\) for every \(\theta\), where \(k_V(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-V(\theta,x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty]\). For probability measures \(\mu,\nu\) on the state space with finite second moments, \(W_2(\mu,\nu)=\inf_\pi\bigl(\int\|u-v\|^2\,\pi(du,dv)\bigr)^{1/2}\), the infimum over all couplings \(\pi\) of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). The innovations are independent standard Gaussian, independent of the initialization if every coordinate \(\xi_{k,a}\) has the law \(N(0,1)\), the family \((\xi_{k,a})_{k\ge0,\,a}\) of all coordinates is mutually independent, and \(Z_0\) is independent of the sequence \((\xi_k)_{k\ge0}\).

Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), \(m>0\), \(\eta>0\), \(\gamma>0\) and \(L_1\ge0\). Let \(g_1\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient; let \(e\) be differentiable and convex with \(\eta^{-1}\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(P\) be a map of the pair space with \(\nabla e=\eta^{-1}(I-P)\). Put \(V=g_1+e\), \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), and assume

\[\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\eta}.\]

Let \(\theta^\star\) be a marginal maximizer of \(V\). Let \(Z_0,\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) be square-integrable random states with independent standard Gaussian innovations independent of the initialization, let \(\rho_n\) be the law of the \(n\)-th MYIPLA iterate and \(\theta_n\) its parameter block. Then for every \(n\ge0\)

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta^\star\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

Proof. Regularity of \(V\). By the first step, \(V\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, and \(\nabla V\) is \((L_1+\eta^{-1})=L_\eta\)-Lipschitz; \(V\) is differentiable as a sum of differentiable functions.

Identification of the laws. By the previous step (with \(L=L_\eta\)), \(\rho_n\) is the law of the \(n\)-th IPLA iterate for \(V\), with the same initialization and innovations.

The IPLA bound. The IPLA estimate with sharp parameter concentration applies to a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex pair potential with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(m>0\), step \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L)\), a marginal maximizer and Gaussian innovations as above. Its hypotheses hold for \(V\) with \(L=L_\eta\), and its conclusion is the displayed inequality. In that estimate the three terms have the following origin: the lifted potential \(F_V\) is \(Nm\)-strongly convex with \(NL_\eta\)-Lipschitz gradient on a space of dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\), and the Gaussian Euler step with step \(\gamma/N\) contracts the Wasserstein distance to \(\pi_{N,V}\) by \(1-m\gamma\) per iteration up to a discretization error, which gives the second and third terms; the parameter marginal of \(\pi_{N,V}\) has second moment at most \(d_\theta/(Nm)\) about \(\theta^\star\), which gives the first term after projecting onto the parameter block. \(\square\)

The bound concerns the maximizer \(\theta^\star\) of the smoothed marginal likelihood. The smoothing parameter enters through \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), both in the step restriction and in the discretization term: a smaller \(\eta\) forces a smaller step.

steps.title: The theorem for the Moreau envelope
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N\ge1\), \(\eta>0\), \(L_1\ge0\), let \(g_1\) be differentiable with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(g_2\) be convex and bounded below on the (finite-dimensional) pair space. Let \(P_\eta\) be the proximal map of \(g_2\), \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), and let \(\rho_n\) be the law of the \(n\)-th MYIPLA iterate with proximal map \(P_\eta\), smoothing parameter \(\eta\), any step \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and square-integrable initialization and innovations. Then for every \(n\):

  1. \(\rho_n\) is a probability measure;
  2. \(\int\|\theta(z)-\vartheta\|^2\,\rho_n(dz)<\infty\) for every \(\vartheta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\);
  3. if in addition \(g_1\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\) with \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), \(\theta^\star_\eta\) is a marginal maximizer of \(V_\eta\), and the innovations are independent standard Gaussian and independent of the initialization, then \[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta^\star_\eta\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V_\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

Proof. By the Moreau envelope section, under the stated hypotheses on \(g_2\) and \(\eta>0\): \(e=g_2^\eta\) is differentiable and convex, \(\nabla e=\eta^{-1}(I-P_\eta)\), and \(\nabla e\) is \(\eta^{-1}\)-Lipschitz (the residual is \(\eta^{-1}\)-Lipschitz). With \(P=P_\eta\) all hypotheses of the previous two steps that concern \(e\) and \(P\) are therefore satisfied, and \(\nabla(g_1+e)\) is \(L_\eta\)-Lipschitz by the first step.

(a) By the second step, \(\rho_n\) is the pushforward of the probability measure \(Q\) under a measurable map \(Y_n\), so \(\rho_n(\text{whole space})=Q(Y_n^{-1}(\text{whole space}))=Q(\Omega)=1\).

(b) is part (b) of the second step.

(c) is the previous step with \(e=g_2^\eta\) and \(P=P_\eta\). \(\square\)

ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.title: MYIPLA about the marginal maximizer of the original nonsmooth model
ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.summary:
Let \(U=g_1+g_2\) be a pair potential on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), where \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient (\(m>0\)), and \(g_2\) is convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz. Combined with the MYIPLA estimate of the previous section and Minkowski's inequality, this gives the main bound for MYIPLA relative to the original model: under Gaussian innovations independent of a square-integrable initialization and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\),

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V_\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

The smoothing contribution is of order \(\sqrt\eta\). This replaces the smoothing term of Theorem 4.1 of arXiv:2406.14292v3, which was derived from a Taylor expansion and is of linear order in \(\eta\); the linear order is not established here. The discretization term depends on \(\eta\) through \(L_\eta\).

steps.title: The uniform comparison and existence of the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Claim. (a) Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(g_1:E\to\mathbb R\) any function, \(g_2:E\to\mathbb R\) convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz (\(K\ge0\)), and \(\eta>0\). Then for every \(z\in E\)

\[V_\eta(z)\le g_1(z)+g_2(z)\le V_\eta(z)+\frac{\eta K^2}{2},\qquad V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta.\qquad(1)\]

(b) On the pair space, let in addition \(g_1\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\). Then \(U=g_1+g_2\) has a marginal maximizer: there is \(\theta_U\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(k_U(\theta)\le k_U(\theta_U)\) for all \(\theta\), where \(k_U(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\).

Proof. (a) By the Moreau envelope section, \(0\le g_2(z)-g_2^\eta(z)\le\eta K^2/2\). Adding \(g_1(z)\) to the three members of \(g_2^\eta(z)\le g_2(z)\le g_2^\eta(z)+\eta K^2/2\) gives (1).

(b) Fix any \(\eta>0\). The function \(U\) is continuous, because \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(g_2\) is Lipschitz. The comparison potential \(V_\eta\) is differentiable (sum of \(g_1\) and the differentiable envelope) and \(m\)-strongly convex (sum of \(g_1\) and the convex envelope), and \(V_\eta\le U\) by (1). These are exactly the hypotheses of the existence theorem for the original marginal maximizer , which proves (b): the bound \(e^{-U}\le e^{-V_\eta}\) and a Gaussian majorant of \(e^{-V_\eta}\) make \(k_U\) finite, positive, continuous and tending to \(0\) as \(\|\theta\|\to\infty\), so \(k_U\) attains its maximum. \(\square\)

The smoothing parameter in (b) is auxiliary; any \(\eta>0\) provides the required smooth lower comparison potential.

steps.title: The distance between the original and the smoothed marginal maximizers
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g_1\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), let \(g_2\) be convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz, and \(\eta>0\). If \(\theta_U\) is a marginal maximizer of \(U=g_1+g_2\) and \(\theta_\eta\) is a marginal maximizer of \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), then

\[\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}} .\]

Proof. By (1) of the previous step, \(V_\eta\le U\le V_\eta+\delta\) with \(\delta=\eta K^2/2\). As in the previous step, \(U\) is continuous and \(V_\eta\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. The marginal-center comparison states that, under exactly these conditions, any marginal maximizers satisfy \(\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{2\delta/m}\). Its proof compares the marginal potentials \(\varphi_W=-\log k_W\): integrating \(e^{-V_\eta-\delta}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V_\eta}\) over the latent variable gives \(\varphi_{V_\eta}\le\varphi_U\le\varphi_{V_\eta}+\delta\), the marginal potential \(\varphi_{V_\eta}\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with minimizer \(\theta_\eta\), and therefore

\[\frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|^2\le\varphi_{V_\eta}(\theta_U)-\varphi_{V_\eta}(\theta_\eta)\le\varphi_U(\theta_U)-\varphi_{V_\eta}(\theta_\eta)\le\varphi_U(\theta_\eta)-\varphi_{V_\eta}(\theta_\eta)\le\delta .\]

With \(\delta=\eta K^2/2\), \(2\delta/m=\eta K^2/m\). \(\square\)

The bound is of order \(\sqrt\eta\). No second derivative of \(U\) and no Taylor expansion of the envelope are used.

steps.title: The MYIPLA error about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,Q)\) be a probability space and \(N\ge1\). Let \(g_1\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g_2\) convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz, with \(L_1,K\ge0\). Let \(m,\eta,\gamma>0\), \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), and

\[\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\eta}.\]

Let \(\theta_U\) be a marginal maximizer of \(U=g_1+g_2\) and \(\theta_\eta\) one of \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\). Let the initialization \(Z_0\) and innovations \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots\) be square-integrable random states such that all innovation coordinates are independent standard Gaussian and \(Z_0\) is independent of the innovation sequence. Let \(\rho_n\) be the law of the \(n\)-th MYIPLA iterate with proximal map \(P_\eta\) of \(g_2\), and \(\theta_n\) its parameter block. Then for every \(n\ge0\)

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V_\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

Proof. Finiteness. By the previous section, \(\rho_n\) is a probability measure and \(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2=\int\|\theta(z)-\theta_\eta\|^2\rho_n(dz)<\infty\).

Change of center. By Minkowski's inequality in \(L^2(\rho_n)\) applied to \(\theta(z)-\theta_U=(\theta(z)-\theta_\eta)+(\theta_\eta-\theta_U)\), in the form proved in (which requires the finite moment just established),

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}+\|\theta_\eta-\theta_U\|.\qquad(1)\]

The two terms. By the previous step, \(\|\theta_\eta-\theta_U\|=\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\). By the MYIPLA estimate for the Moreau envelope of the previous section, applied with the smoothed marginal maximizer \(\theta_\eta\),

\[\Bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi_{N,V_\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}N}\,\sqrt\gamma .\]

Inserting both bounds into (1) proves the claim. \(\square\)

The four terms are the smoothing bias, the equilibrium spread of the parameter marginal, the contracted initial transport distance, and the discretization error. Decreasing \(\eta\) decreases the first term but increases \(L_\eta\), hence the last term and the restriction on \(\gamma\). The existence of \(\theta_U\) was proved in the first step, and a marginal maximizer \(\theta_\eta\) of the smooth strongly convex potential \(V_\eta\) exists by ; the theorem itself takes both points as given maximizers.

ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.title: Changing the center of a projected quadratic error
ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.summary:
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on a real normed space \(E\), \(T:E\to F\) a continuous linear map into a real normed space \(F\), and \(a\in F\). The projected quadratic error of \(\mu\) about the center \(a\) is

\[R_\mu(a)=\Bigl(\int_E\|Tx-a\|^2\,\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty],\]

with the convention \(R_\mu(a)=\infty\) when \(x\mapsto Tx\) is not measurable for \(\mu\). By Minkowski's inequality, \(R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|b-a\|\) for any two centers. Hence a finite error about one center implies a finite error about every center, and then the inequality holds between the ordinary square-root integrals. The result is used with \(T\) the projection onto the parameter block, to move the center from the smoothed marginal maximizer to the original one.

steps.title: Minkowski's inequality for the change of center
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\), \(T:E\to F\) continuous and linear, and \(a,b\in F\). Then

\[R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|b-a\|\qquad\text{in }[0,\infty],\qquad(1)\]

and if \(R_\mu(b)<\infty\), then \(R_\mu(a)<\infty\).

Proof. For every \(x\), \(Tx-a=(Tx-b)+(b-a)\). Minkowski's inequality in \(L^2(\mu)\), which holds for functions with values in a normed space and with norms in \([0,\infty]\), gives

\[R_\mu(a)=\bigl\|(T\cdot-b)+(b-a)\bigr\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le\|T\cdot-b\|_{L^2(\mu)}+\|b-a\|_{L^2(\mu)},\]

where in the last term \(b-a\) denotes the constant function. Its \(L^2(\mu)\) norm is \(\bigl(\int\|b-a\|^2\,d\mu\bigr)^{1/2}=\|b-a\|\,\mu(E)^{1/2}=\|b-a\|\), because \(\mu(E)=1\). This proves (1). If \(R_\mu(b)<\infty\), the right-hand side of (1) is finite, hence so is \(R_\mu(a)\). If \(x\mapsto Tx\) is not measurable, both errors are infinite and (1) holds trivially. \(\square\)

For a finite measure of total mass \(M\) the constant term would be \(\sqrt M\,\|b-a\|\); the coefficient \(1\) uses \(M=1\). The inequality is proved before any finiteness is known, so finiteness about \(a\) is a conclusion, not a hypothesis.

ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.title: Uniform potential gaps and the displacement of marginal maximizers
ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.summary:
Let \(U\) and \(V\) be real functions on the pair space \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\) with \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), where \(U\) is continuous (and possibly nonsmooth) and \(V\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\). For a pair function \(W\) define the marginal integral and the marginal potential

\[k_W(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-W(\theta,x)}\,dx,\qquad\varphi_W(\theta)=-\log k_W(\theta).\]

A marginal maximizer of \(W\) is a maximizer of \(k_W\), i.e. a maximizer of the marginal likelihood in the latent-variable model with joint density proportional to \(e^{-W}\). This section proves: \(k_U\) is positive, finite and continuous and has a maximizer; \(\varphi_V\le\varphi_U\le\varphi_V+\delta\); a marginal maximizer of \(U\) minimizes \(\varphi_U\); and any marginal maximizers \(\theta_U\) of \(U\) and \(\theta_V\) of \(V\) satisfy

\[\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{m}} .\]

The tools are the quadratic growth of a strongly convex function at its minimizer, monotonicity of the integral, a Gaussian majorant of \(e^{-V}\), dominated convergence, and the strong convexity of \(\varphi_V\) (a consequence of the Prékopa–Leindler inequality, proved in the IPLA development). No derivative of \(U\) and no expansion in \(\delta\) are used. With \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), \(U=g_1+g_2\) and \(\delta=\eta K^2/2\) this gives the smoothing bias \(\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\).

steps.title: Quadratic growth at the minimizer of a strongly convex function
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(m\ge0\), \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) \(m\)-strongly convex, and \(z\in H\) a global minimizer of \(F\). Then for every \(x\in H\)

\[F(z)+\frac m2\|x-z\|^2\le F(x).\]

Proof. Fix \(x\) and put \(A=\frac m2\|x-z\|^2\ge0\) and \(G=F(x)-F(z)\ge0\) (minimality). We show \(A\le G\). Suppose instead \(G<A\); then \(A>G\ge0\). Put

\[b=\frac{A-G}{2A},\qquad\text{so that}\quad0<b\le\frac12,\qquad b\cdot2A=A-G.\qquad(1)\]

Strong convexity with weights \(1-b\) and \(b\) at the points \(z\) and \(x\) gives

\[F\bigl((1-b)z+bx\bigr)\le(1-b)F(z)+bF(x)-b(1-b)\frac m2\|x-z\|^2=F(z)+bG-b(1-b)A.\]

Minimality of \(z\) gives \(F(z)\le F((1-b)z+bx)\). Hence \(0\le bG-b(1-b)A\), and dividing by \(b>0\), \((1-b)A\le G\). By (1), \((1-b)A=A-bA=A-\frac{A-G}2=\frac{A+G}2\). Thus \(\frac{A+G}2\le G\), i.e. \(A\le G\), contradicting \(G<A\). Therefore \(A\le G\), which is the claim. \(\square\)

The argument uses only the strong-convexity inequality and global minimality; \(F\) need not be differentiable.

steps.title: Comparison of the marginal integrals and the marginal potentials
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U,V\) be real functions on the pair space and \(\delta\in\mathbb R\) with \(V(w)\le U(w)\le V(w)+\delta\) for every pair \(w\). Fix \(\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\).

  1. For the integrals \(M_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty]\) of the nonnegative functions \(e^{-W(\theta,\cdot)}\) (finite or not), \[M_U(\theta)\le M_V(\theta)\le e^\delta M_U(\theta).\qquad(1)\]
  2. If moreover \(U\) is continuous and \(V\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), then \(k_U(\theta)\) and \(k_V(\theta)\) are finite and positive, and \[\varphi_V(\theta)\le\varphi_U(\theta)\le\varphi_V(\theta)+\delta.\qquad(2)\]

Proof. (a) Since \(-U\le-V\) and the exponential is increasing, \(e^{-U(\theta,x)}\le e^{-V(\theta,x)}\) for every \(x\); monotonicity of the integral of nonnegative functions gives \(M_U(\theta)\le M_V(\theta)\). Since \(U\le V+\delta\), \(-V-\delta\le-U\), so \(e^{-V(\theta,x)}=e^\delta e^{-V(\theta,x)-\delta}\le e^\delta e^{-U(\theta,x)}\). Integrating and taking the finite constant \(e^\delta\) out of the integral gives \(M_V(\theta)\le e^\delta M_U(\theta)\).

(b) Integrability. Since \(V\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \(V(w)\ge V(0)+\langle\nabla V(0),w\rangle+\frac m2\|w\|^2\), and by Young's inequality \(\langle\nabla V(0),w\rangle\ge-\|\nabla V(0)\|^2/m-\frac m4\|w\|^2\). Hence, with \(\|w\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2\ge\|x\|^2\) for \(w=(\theta,x)\),

\[e^{-V(\theta,x)}\le C\,e^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2},\qquad C=\exp\Bigl(\frac{\|\nabla V(0)\|^2}{m}-V(0)\Bigr),\qquad(3)\]

and the right-hand side is integrable in \(x\) (a Gaussian function). So \(e^{-V(\theta,\cdot)}\) is integrable . The function \(x\mapsto e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) is continuous, hence measurable, and bounded by \(e^{-V(\theta,x)}\); it is therefore integrable.

Positivity and comparison. Both integrands are strictly positive and integrable, so \(k_U(\theta)>0\) and \(k_V(\theta)>0\). The pointwise inequalities of (a) and monotonicity of the integral give \(k_U(\theta)\le k_V(\theta)\le e^\delta k_U(\theta)\).

Logarithms. The logarithm is increasing on \((0,\infty)\). From \(k_U\le k_V\), \(\log k_U(\theta)\le\log k_V(\theta)\), i.e. \(\varphi_V(\theta)\le\varphi_U(\theta)\). From \(k_V\le e^\delta k_U\), \(\log k_V(\theta)\le\delta+\log k_U(\theta)\), i.e. \(\varphi_U(\theta)\le\varphi_V(\theta)+\delta\). \(\square\)

The additive gap \(\delta\) passes unchanged from the potentials to the marginal potentials, because the logarithm is taken after the integration.

steps.title: Integrability, continuity and a maximizer of the original marginal
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be continuous, \(V\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), and \(V\le U\) on the pair space. Then:

  1. for every \(\theta\), \(x\mapsto e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) is integrable on \(\mathbb R^{d_x}\);
  2. \(k_U\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\);
  3. \(U\) has a marginal maximizer: there is \(\theta^\star\) with \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\le\int e^{-U(\theta^\star,x)}\,dx\) for all \(\theta\).

Proof. (a) As in the previous step, \(e^{-U(\theta,\cdot)}\) is measurable and dominated by the integrable function \(e^{-V(\theta,\cdot)}\).

(b) We apply the dominated convergence theorem for parameter-dependent integrals: if \(f(\theta,\cdot)\) is measurable for each \(\theta\), \(|f(\theta,x)|\le h(x)\) for all \(\theta\) and \(x\) with \(h\) integrable, and \(\theta\mapsto f(\theta,x)\) is continuous for every \(x\), then \(\theta\mapsto\int f(\theta,x)\,dx\) is continuous. Take \(f(\theta,x)=e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) and \(h(x)=Ce^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2}\) with the constant \(C\) of (3) in the previous step: then \(f(\theta,x)\le e^{-V(\theta,x)}\le h(x)\) for all \(\theta\), \(h\) is integrable, and continuity of \(U\) gives continuity of \(\theta\mapsto f(\theta,x)\).

(c) Decay. By (3) with the full norm \(\|w\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2\), \(e^{-V(\theta,x)}\le Ce^{-\frac m4\|\theta\|^2}e^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2}\), so \(k_V(\theta)\to0\) as \(\|\theta\|\to\infty\) . Since \(0\le k_U\le k_V\), also \(k_U(\theta)\to0\).

A maximum. \(k_U(0)>0\), because the integrand is positive and integrable. By the decay there is \(R>0\) with \(k_U(\theta)<k_U(0)\) whenever \(\|\theta\|>R\). The closed ball of radius \(R\) is compact and \(k_U\) is continuous by (b), so \(k_U\) attains a maximum on it at some \(\theta^\star\); then \(k_U(\theta^\star)\ge k_U(0)>k_U(\theta)\) for \(\|\theta\|>R\), so \(\theta^\star\) is a global maximizer of \(k_U\).

Extended integrals. For an integrable nonnegative function the integral in \([0,\infty]\) equals the real integral, so \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx=k_U(\theta)\) in both senses, and \(\theta^\star\) is a marginal maximizer. \(\square\)

steps.title: Minimality of the marginal potential and the displacement of maximizers
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be continuous, \(V\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\).

  1. If \(V\le U\) and \(\theta^\star\) is a marginal maximizer of \(U\), then \(\varphi_U(\theta^\star)\le\varphi_U(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\).
  2. If \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), \(\theta_U\) is a marginal maximizer of \(U\) and \(\theta_V\) a marginal maximizer of \(V\), then \[\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\frac{2\delta}m,\qquad\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}m}.\]

Proof. (a) By the previous step, \(k_U(\theta)\) is finite and positive and equals the extended integral. The maximizer property gives \(k_U(\theta)\le k_U(\theta^\star)\), and since the logarithm is increasing on \((0,\infty)\), \(-\log k_U(\theta^\star)\le-\log k_U(\theta)\).

(b) Four facts are combined. By (a), \(\theta_U\) minimizes \(\varphi_U\); in particular

\[\varphi_U(\theta_U)\le\varphi_U(\theta_V).\qquad(1)\]

For the smooth strongly convex \(V\), a marginal maximizer minimizes \(\varphi_V\) , and \(\varphi_V\) is \(m\)-strongly convex (integration over the latent variable preserves strong log-concavity, by the Prékopa–Leindler inequality). The quadratic growth of the first step at the minimizer \(\theta_V\) gives

\[\varphi_V(\theta_V)+\frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\varphi_V(\theta_U).\qquad(2)\]

By (2) of the second step at \(\theta_U\) and at \(\theta_V\),

\[\varphi_V(\theta_U)\le\varphi_U(\theta_U),\qquad\varphi_U(\theta_V)\le\varphi_V(\theta_V)+\delta.\qquad(3)\]

Chaining (2), the first inequality of (3), (1) and the second inequality of (3),

\[\frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\varphi_V(\theta_U)-\varphi_V(\theta_V)\le\varphi_U(\theta_U)-\varphi_V(\theta_V)\le\varphi_U(\theta_V)-\varphi_V(\theta_V)\le\delta .\]

Multiplying by \(2/m>0\) gives the first bound. In particular \(2\delta/m\ge0\), and since the square root is increasing on \([0,\infty)\) and \(\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|\ge0\), taking square roots gives the second bound. \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(V\le U\le V+\delta\) itself forces \(\delta\ge0\). Only \(V\) needs to be differentiable; the minimality of \(\theta_U\) for \(\varphi_U\) is used only through (1).

ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.title: PIPULA for the full envelope and its smoothed marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.summary: PIPULA applies the full-potential pairwise proximal map and then adds Gaussian noise. The residual identity makes it Euler Langevin for the full Moreau envelope at the same scale. The envelope has reduced curvature \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\). Assume the original potential \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below, with \(m,\gamma>0\). No global Lipschitz assumption is imposed on \(U\). The resulting estimate concerns the marginal maximizer of \(U^\gamma\) and retains the scale dependence of the generic Euler error.

steps.title: The full-envelope curvature and admissible step
steps.body:
Set \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)>0\). The inequality \(\gamma m_\gamma=m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)\le1\) gives \(\gamma(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\le2\), equivalently \(\gamma\le2/(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\). Positivity of the denominators justifies the multiplications and divisions.

More specifically, \(m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)<1\) implies \(\gamma m_\gamma+1\le2\). Since the envelope gradient constant is \(1/\gamma\), this is precisely the required Euler restriction. The contraction factor is \(1-m_\gamma\gamma=1/(1+m\gamma)>0\). These facts follow from strong convexity of the original potential and envelope regularity, without a global Lipschitz bound on the original potential’s values.

steps.body:
In the MYIPLA update set \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\). Proximal optimality gives \(P_\gamma=I-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma\), so the resulting recursion is IPLA for \(U^\gamma\).

The pointwise identity \(P_\gamma(v)=v-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma(v)\), applied to every pair, gives the scaled Euler drift. Adding the same Gaussian vector after proximity gives the PIPULA update. Equality at initialization and at each successor proves equality of all finite iterates; their measurable pushforwards therefore agree as probability laws.
