steps.title: The proved estimate about the smoothed marginal center
steps.body:
The update specialization \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\) identifies PIPULA with full-envelope IPLA. The source’s claim about error relative to the original marginal maximizer requires additional analysis: its proximal inner-product deficit \(\mu\) gives envelope-gradient monotonicity coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\) because the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). A scale-uniform discretization estimate and the source’s rate relative to the original marginal maximizer are not established by substituting smoothness \(1/\gamma\) into a generic Euler bound.

The proved estimate instead assumes a bounded-below \(m\)-strongly convex full potential. For \(\gamma>0\) its envelope curvature is \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and its gradient constant is \(1/\gamma\). The generic error term is \((33/20)(1/(\gamma m_\gamma))\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\), which diverges as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). It therefore does not reproduce the claimed rate \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) relative to the original marginal maximizer.

Write \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\), let \(\Pi_{N,\gamma}\) be the envelope Gibbs law, and let \(\theta_\gamma\) be its marginal maximizer. Sharp concentration and the Gaussian particle estimate give

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\gamma\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm_\gamma}}+(1-m_\gamma\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{\gamma^{-1}}{m_\gamma}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The theorem uses gradient constant \(\gamma^{-1}\). For a separately denoted envelope scale, the curvature is \(m_\eta=m/(1+m\eta)\) rather than \(m\) and the gradient constant is \(1/\eta\); the required restriction is \(\gamma\le2/(m_\eta+1/\eta)\). At equal proximal and Euler scales, the preceding algebra proves it automatically. The equilibrium radius uses this reduced curvature, and the error coefficient uses \((1/\gamma)/m_\gamma\). Consequently the valid finite-step estimate is about the smoothed center and does not prove vanishing error as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). A uniform conclusion relative to the original marginal maximizer would require a stronger envelope analysis.

ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.title: Bounded fields and positive global strong monotonicity
ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.summary: A globally bounded vector field on a nontrivial real Hilbert space cannot have a positive global strong-monotonicity constant. The Moreau gradient of a globally Lipschitz convex function is bounded. Hence the conjunction of full-potential value Lipschitzness and a positive global proximal-residual deficit is inconsistent. The conclusion concerns that literal conjunction of assumptions; it does not apply to a decomposition in which only the nonsmooth summand is Lipschitz.

steps.title: Incompatibility of boundedness and positive global monotonicity
steps.body:
Assume \(\|R(x)\|\le K\) and \(c\|x-y\|^2\le\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\) with \(c>0\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality give \(c\|x-y\|^2\le2K\|x-y\|\). A nonzero direction can be scaled to have length greater than \(2K/c\), contradicting this bound.

In the alternative notation \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) and \(\langle b(x)-b(y),x-y\rangle\ge q\|x-y\|^2\) with \(q>0\) imply \(q\|x-y\|\le2K\) for every distinct pair. Explicitly choose separation \(r>2K/c\). Strong monotonicity bounds the inner product below by \(cr^2\), while boundedness bounds it above by \(2Kr\). Division by \(r\) gives \(cr\le2K\). A nontrivial space has arbitrarily large such separations \(r\), so the assumptions cannot both hold. The nontrivial-space qualification is essential.

\[ \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\|x-y\|^2 \le\langle x-y,R_\gamma(x)-R_\gamma(y)\rangle \le2K\|x-y\|. \]

The preceding obstruction contradicts these simultaneous global conditions on a nontrivial space. If the Lipschitz assumption instead concerns the nonsmooth term in an independent decomposition \(U=g_1+g_2\), it does not make the full \(U\) Lipschitz and the contradiction does not follow.

The residual \(R_\gamma=(I-P_\gamma)/\gamma\) is bounded in the first reading, while the deficit makes it strongly monotone with coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\). Under \(\mu>0\) these are incompatible. This is a conditional consistency result about the specified assumptions, not a general refutation of the source corollary. The separate full-potential PIPULA theorem assumes strong convexity and a lower bound without global value Lipschitzness.

ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.title: Sharp Gibbs concentration by dilation
ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.summary: Let \(F\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex in dimension \(d\), with \(q>0\) and global minimizer \(z\). A contraction toward the minimizer compares the Gibbs partition with its unnormalized second moment. The left derivative at unit dilation gives the dimension-over-curvature bound. Gaussian domination ensures all integrals are finite, and only an explicit scalar expression is differentiated; no derivative of the potential is required.

steps.title: The partition comparison under radial contraction
steps.body:
Strong convexity and minimality give \(F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\frac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2\) for \(0<r<1\). Exponentiate and use \(e^u\ge1+u\). The dilation \(x\mapsto z+r(x-z)\) has determinant \(r^d\), so integration gives

\[Z+\frac q2(1-r^2)M\le r^{-d}Z,\qquad Z=\int e^{-F},\quad M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F}.\]

In the notation \(w(x)=e^{-F(x)}\), \(Z=\int w\), \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2w(x)\,dx\), and \(d=\dim H\), Gaussian domination first proves integrability of \(w\) and \(\|x-z\|^2w\). Strong convexity combined with quadratic growth at the mode gives

\[F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2.\]

Using \(e^u\ge1+u\) after exponentiation gives

\[w(z+r(x-z))\ge w(x)+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2w(x).\]

Indeed the strong-convexity segment from the minimizer to \(x\) contributes radial deficit \(q(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2/2\). Inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\) turns it into a density-plus-moment bound. The determinant is \(r^d\), so the integral of the dilated density is \(r^{-d}Z\). This proves the partition comparison with all terms finite.

ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.title: Sharp parameter concentration and the IPLA RMS bound
ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.summary: Apply the continuous-potential concentration estimate to the parameter marginal, whose curvature has factor \(N\) from particle count. For a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex pair potential \(U\) with \(m>0\), Prékopa–Leindler gives the marginal curvature. Its \(N\)-power target has curvature \(Nm\), so its parameter second moment is at most \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). steps.title: Sharp concentration of the parameter marginal
steps.body:
For continuous \(a\)-strongly convex potential \(f\) with minimizer \(x_\star\), the dilation argument gives

\[ \int\|x-x_\star\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le\frac d a, \qquad\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dx. \]

Only continuity, strong convexity, and a minimizing point are needed; no nonsmooth integration-by-parts formula is assumed. Prékopa–Leindler gives strong convexity of the parameter marginal potential. Raising the marginal likelihood to its \(N\)-th power multiplies that curvature by \(N\). Thus

\[ W_2(\Pi_{\lambda,N}^{\theta},\delta_{\theta_{\lambda,\star}}) \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}. \]

This is the factor in the source’s equilibrium estimate. The earlier radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) was a valid weaker bound.

The parameter density is proportional to \(M(\theta)^N\) and has negative log potential \(NF(\theta)\). Its curvature is \(Nm\), with minimizer \(\theta_*\). The sharp theorem in dimension \(d_\theta\) gives \(\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N\le d_\theta/(Nm)\). In the equivalent notation, density \(e^{-N\Phi}\) has curvature \(Nm\), so dimension \(d_\theta\) gives second moment \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). The exact projection identity transfers that same moment to the full Gibbs law; its nonnegative square root is the equilibrium root mean square radius.

steps.title: Projection norms and Gaussian moments
steps.body:
The parameter projection satisfies \(\|P_\theta z\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\) and hence \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). Linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb E P_\theta\xi=0\); the unit second moment of each standard Gaussian coordinate gives \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta\xi\|^2=d_\theta\).

In the coordinate expansion \(\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\), each summand is integrable because the Gaussian vector belongs to \(L^2\). The identities \(\mathbb E z_j^2=1\) and \(\mathbb E P_\theta Z=P_\theta\mathbb EZ=0\) therefore give \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta Z\|^2=d_\theta\) by a finite sum. No factor \(N\) occurs: the projection retains exactly \(d_\theta\) scalar coordinates and their variances sum to \(d_\theta\). The particle count enters only when this noise block is multiplied by amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\).

steps.title: Nonexpansiveness of the averaged pair map
steps.body:
Jensen’s inequality for the averaged parameter difference and the exact latent squared scaling give

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-\operatorname{Pair}_P(w)\|^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|P(J_i z)-P(J_i w)\|^2.\]

If \(P\) is nonexpansive, each squared summand is at most \(\|J_i(z-w)\|^2\). Their sum is \(N\|z-w\|^2\), so the averaged map is nonexpansive.

Explicitly put \(A_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\) and \(\Delta_i=P(A_i z)-P(A_i w)\). The parameter inequality is \(N\|\overline\Delta_\theta\|^2\le\sum_i\|\Delta_{i,\theta}\|^2\), while the latent differences are rescaled by \(N^{-1/2}\). Thus

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}P(z)-\operatorname{Pair}P(w)\|^2\le\frac1N\sum_i\|\Delta_i\|^2.\]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P\) and identity \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-w)\|^2=N\|z-w\|^2\) give the unit full-state Lipschitz bound. Positivity of \(N\) justifies division and rescaling. The argument compares two averaged outputs and does not assume that either minimizes a shared-state proximal objective.

steps.title: The averaged potential’s value Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Put \(G(z)=F_g(z)/N\). Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite average and \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) imply \(N^{-1}\sum_i\|J_i v\|\le\|v\|\). Applying the pairwise value Lipschitz estimate therefore gives

\[|G(z)-G(w)|\le\frac KN\sum_i\|J_i(z-w)\|\le K\|z-w\|.\]

The latent scaling \(N^{-1/2}\) makes the average pair squared distance equal to the state squared distance. Consequently the averaged physical-time potential \(G=F_g/N\) retains value Lipschitz constant \(K\). This bound ensures integrability of its values at square-integrable random states.
steps.lean:
Let \(\bar f_N(z)=N^{-1}\sum_i f(A_i z)\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the replication identity give \[\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|\le\left(\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|^2\right)^{1/2}=\|v\|.\] Applying \(|f(a)-f(b)|\le K\|a-b\|\) to each pair and summing proves \(|\bar f_N(z)-\bar f_N(w)|\le K\|z-w\|\). The declarations separate the average norm estimate from the value estimate so that the particle scaling can be checked independently.

ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.title: Uniform Moreau gaps in scaled particle coordinates
ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.summary: The lifted envelope gradient has norm at most \(NK\), and its uniform potential gap is at most \(N\eta K^2/2\). These follow by summing the single-pair value estimates and are different from gradient variation with constant involving \(1/\eta\). Write \(F_g(z)=\sum_i g(J_i z)\) with \(N>0\). If \(g\) is convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz, the Moreau value Lipschitz bound yields a gradient-magnitude estimate uniform over positive smoothing parameters.

steps.title: The lifted value bound and envelope-gradient magnitude
steps.body:
The averaged potential has value Lipschitz constant \(K\). Multiplication by \(N\) gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(F_g)\le NK\). Since the envelope retains single-pair value constant \(K\), its lifted sum \(F_{g^\eta}\) has constant \(NK\). Differentiability therefore bounds its gradient norm by \(NK\) for every \(\eta>0\).

Equivalently multiplication by \(N\) gives lifted value constant \(NK\). The envelope’s single-pair constant \(K\) yields \(\|\nabla V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\|\le NK\). This uses the norm bound for the derivative of a Lipschitz function, rather than the gradient Lipschitz constant \(N/\eta\), and is consequently uniform as \(\eta\downarrow0\). In the averaged notation the constants are \(K\) and \(NK\) for the full sum, giving \(\|\nabla F_{g_2^\eta}\|\le NK\) independently of \(\eta\). Rapid spatial variation of the gradient does not change this bound on its magnitude.

steps.title: The summed envelope gap and split-potential identity
steps.body:
Apply \(0\le g-g^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\) at each pair and sum the finite inequalities:

\[0\le F_g(z)-F_{g^\eta}(z)\le N\eta K^2/2.\]

Distributivity also gives the function identity \(F_{g_1+g_2^\eta}=F_{g_1}+F_{g_2^\eta}\). In nonsmooth-component notation the bound \(0\le g_2-g_2^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\) has \(N\) summands, so

\[0\le V_N^{(2)}-V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\le N\eta K^2/2.\]

Expanding \(V_N(g_1+g_2^\eta)\) and distributing the sum gives \(V_N(g_1)+V_N(g_2^\eta)\). Each nonnegative gap is at most \(\eta K^2/2\); summing \(N\) such gaps proves the displayed total gap directly. Differentiating the sum identity, under the established regularity, separates the smooth and envelope reference forces in the splitting argument.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.title: Integrated quadratic and convex-energy estimates
ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.summary: Apply the deterministic energy estimate to \(L^2\) random vectors. Lipschitz growth makes the scalar potential values integrable, and square integrability makes all squared-distance terms integrable. Weighted Young inequalities control the smooth local defect without losing the squared contraction. Integrated convex supports retain the perturbation-force pairing in a form that can be combined with the expected potential difference.

steps.title: Weighted Young inequality and squared contraction
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), expansion and \((t\|v\|-\|r\|)^2\ge0\) give

\[\|v+r\|^2\le(1+t)\|v\|^2+(1+t^{-1})\|r\|^2.\]

If \(0<t\le1\) and \(\|v\|\le(1-t)\|e\|\), the inequality \((1+t)(1-t)^2\le1-t\) leaves a squared contraction with coefficient one minus the parameter. The identity \(\|v+r+b\|^2=\|v+r\|^2+2\langle v+r+b,b\rangle-\|b\|^2\) separately retains the force cross term.

Choosing the Young parameter as \(mh\) gives \((1+mh)(1-mh)^2\le1-mh\) under \(mh\le1\), while multiplying the squared local defect by \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). Keeping the integrated perturbation force in its inner product permits its convex-energy contribution to combine with the proximal energy difference, rather than estimating each term by an unrelated norm bound.
steps.lean:
Expanding \(\|v+r\|^2\) and using \(2\langle v,r\rangle\le t\|v\|^2+t^{-1}\|r\|^2\) gives the weighted inequality. If \(\|v\|\le(1-t)\|e\|\), \(0<t\le1\), then \((1+t)(1-t)^2\le1-t\). This is the scalar inequality proved in hf; it keeps a linear contraction in the squared error instead of doubling the leading term. The final identity rearranges \(\|v+r+b\|^2\) with its cross term paired against the final error, the form needed for convex-energy cancellation.

steps.title: Integrability of potential and quadratic terms
steps.body:
For globally \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function \(f\), subtract \(f(0)\). The centered growth is at most \(K\|X\|\), so \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\) on a probability space. The \(L^2\) norm satisfies \(\|X\|_2^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\).

For observable \(f\), the direct bound is \(|f(X)|\le K\|X\|+|f(0)|\). Thus an \(L^2\) state gives \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). Centering \(f\) justifies the composition estimate. The \(L^2\) inner product and identity \(\langle X,X\rangle=\|X\|^2\) give \(\|X\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\). More generally, bound \(|f(x)|\le|f(0)|+K\|x\|\) makes composition with an \(L^2\) state an \(L^2\) function. Squared differences of \(L^2\) states are also integrable. Hence the potential and quadratic expectations below are finite, and linearity may be applied without subtraction of infinite quantities.

steps.title: The integrated proximal energy inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(\|T(x)-y\|^2\le\|x-y\|^2-2h(f(x)-f(y))+C\) and Lipschitz maps \(T,f\). Substitute \(S,Y\in L^2\) pointwise on a probability-one representative event. The Lipschitz composition represents \(T(S)\) almost surely. Each term is integrable by the preceding growth and moment bounds. Integral monotonicity and linearity therefore give

\[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb E f(S)-\mathbb E f(Y))+C.\]

This is the same energy inequality in \(L^2\). The additive constant is unchanged because the source has mass one. The statement concerns the random output of the actual composed map, as identified by its almost-sure representative.
steps.lean:
Apply the deterministic premise at \((S(\omega),Y(\omega))\). The representative facts for lpDrift and subtraction identify its left side almost everywhere with \(\|T(S)-Y\|^2\). The local facts hn, hfS, hfY prove integrability of both quadratic norms and both potential values. Only then does integral_mono_ae integrate the inequality and distribute its finite terms: \[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb Ef(S)-\mathbb Ef(Y))+C.\] The constant remains \(C\) because \(P\) has mass one.

steps.title: Integrated convex support and the terminal-state difference
steps.body:
The support inequality for a differentiable convex perturbation gives \(\langle S-Y, abla e(Y) angle\le e(S)-e(Y)\) pointwise. Integrability permits the same inequality for the \(L^2\) inner product. For a third vector \(Z\), identity \(S-Z=(S-Y)+(Y-Z)\) leaves additional pairing \(\langle Y-Z, abla e(Y) angle_{L^2}\).

Explicitly, for convex differentiable \(e\) the inequality is \(\langle S-Y, abla e(Y) angle\le e(S)-e(Y)\). The gradient composition and state difference belong to \(L^2\) under the stated bounds, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes their pairing integrable. Integration consequently replaces the reference-force pairing by an expected potential difference, while retaining the endpoint-difference pairing whose future-noise part is shown to vanish separately.
steps.lean:
The pointwise supporting-plane inequality is \(e(S)-e(Y)\ge\langle\nabla e(Y),S-Y\rangle\). Potential integrability follows from value Lipschitzness; inner-product integrability follows from both vectors belonging to \(L^2\), with score Lipschitzness ensuring \(\nabla e(Y)\in L^2\). Integration gives the first declaration. For an endpoint \(Z\), write \(S-Z=(S-Y)+(Y-Z)\) and use linearity of the inner product. This produces the energy difference plus the reference-increment cross term, precisely the two contributions used in splitting_cross_energy_le.

ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.title: Independence under grouping of random variables
ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.summary: Independent source variables may be grouped into an initialized past and a future increment by factoring their joint distributions and reassociating product measures. The results below use joint independence of the specified blocks. Pairwise independence of three separate variables would not imply the required independence of one variable from a pair.

steps.title: An independent family with two indices
steps.body:
Assume \(X\perp Y\) and define \(Z_{\rm false}=X\) and \(Z_{\rm true}=Y\). To verify independence of this two-element family, consider its finite index subsets. The empty subset uses probability mass one, and each singleton gives an identity. For the subset of both indices the condition is exactly \(P(X\in A,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B)\).

Thus two-variable independence is equivalent to the factorization required for the corresponding two-element independent family. No additional independence condition is introduced by this indexing.
steps.lean:
An independent family is defined by factorization for every finite set of indices. For a Boolean index there are four possibilities: neither variable, only \(X\), only \(Y\), or both. The singleton identities are tautological; the empty family has probability one because \(\mu\) is a probability; the two-variable case is exactly the assumed independence of \(X\) and \(Y\). The two membership case splits in Lean exhaust these four possibilities explicitly.

Formal correspondence: iIndepFun_bool_of_indepFun : Two independent random variables form an independent family indexed by Bool . The probability assumption supplies the empty-family identity.

steps.title: Reassociation of a jointly independent triple
steps.body:
Assume measurable variables satisfy \(X\perp(Y,Z)\) and \(Y\perp Z\). Their triple law factors as \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\). Product reassociation gives \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\), while projection gives \(\mu_{(X,Y)}=\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y\). Hence \((X,Y)\perp Z\).

Indeed \(X\) is independent of the entire pair \((Y,Z)\), and \(Y\) and \(Z\) are independent. These hypotheses give \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\), whose reassociation is \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\). This proves independence of \((X,Y)\) and \(Z\). The first two product marginals are the joint law of \((X,Y)\), so the conclusion is \((X,Y)\perp Z\). Equality of measurable pushforward measures proves the statement also for path-valued variables. The hypotheses are stronger than mere pairwise independence.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..title: Orthogonality of future Brownian increments to past observables
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..summary: Assume independent full scalar Brownian paths with measurable evaluations and initialization independent of the entire Brownian family. The integral solution is measurable with respect to initialization and the stopped noise path. A future Brownian increment is independent of this past and centered. Its expected inner product with any square-integrable Lipschitz observable of the reference state is therefore zero. This is an expectation identity, not a samplewise orthogonality claim.

steps.title: Independence of vector stopped past and shifted future
steps.body:
For each scalar coordinate, the shifted future \(B_i(T+s)-B_i(T)\) is independent of the stopped past \(B_i(\min(t,T))\). Independence of the full coordinate paths gives joint independence across these coordinatewise pairs. Selecting and grouping the disjoint past and future indices therefore gives independence of the entire vector-valued past and future path families.

The stopped path records all coordinate values up to time \(t\); the shifted future records increments after \(t\). The resulting independence is between the sigma-algebras generated by these full path blocks. Consequently any measurable function of the entire past is independent of every measurable future increment. This uses full-path independence and Brownian independent increments, rather than unrelated pairwise independence assertions.

steps.title: The pointwise Brownian vector and its square-integrable representative
steps.body:
Define the pointwise vector noise by \(\mathcal B_t=\sqrt2(B(t_+)-B(0))\) with \(t_+=\max(t,0)\). The constructed \(L^2\) Brownian noise agrees almost surely with this expression. Each scalar evaluation is measurable, and finite vector assembly, subtraction, and scaling preserve measurability. Its Gaussian coordinate second moments prove square integrability.

The \(L^2\) class and the pointwise vector thus have the same laws and integrals. Independence and centering may be transferred by their almost-sure equality. The nonnegative-time definition specifies the domain of Brownian evaluation and does not change the positive-time process.

steps.title: Independence of the initialized past from future increments
steps.body:
The stopped Brownian path is independent of the future increment. Initialization is independent of their joint pair. Reassociation of the product law therefore makes the pair consisting of initialization and stopped past independent of the future increment. Any variable measurable with respect to that initialized past inherits the same independence.

A variable only almost everywhere strongly measurable for the past admits a measurable representative with the same law. Almost-sure equality then transfers the conclusion to its \(L^2\) representative. The grouping relation is \((\text{initial},\text{past})\mid\text{future}\). Thus independence for the later reference observable follows from its past measurability and the input assumptions; it is not added as an independent assertion about the solution.

steps.title: Expected orthogonality from independence and centering
steps.body:
Scalar Brownian centering and commutation of finite coordinate projections with integration give \(\mathbb E B_t=0\), and subtraction and scaling give \(\mathbb E\mathcal B_t=0\). For independent \(L^2\) vectors \(X,W\), Cauchy–Schwarz proves integrability of the inner product. Independence and bilinear integration give \(\langle X,W\rangle_{L^2}=\langle\mathbb E X,\mathbb E W\rangle\).

When \(W\) is centered, the latter inner product of means is zero. Thus no norm bound on the other mean is needed: independence and centering give exact expected orthogonality.

steps.title: Orthogonality for observables of the adapted integral solution
steps.body:
The integral-equation construction makes \(Y_t\) measurable for the initialized Brownian past. A Lipschitz observable \(b(Y_t)\) remains measurable for that past and belongs to \(L^2\). Independence of future increments and their zero mean imply

\[\langle b(Y_t),\mathcal B_h-\mathcal B_t\rangle_{L^2}=0,\qquad0\le t\le h.\]

For observable \(b(Y_t)\), both factors are in \(L^2\), so their pairing is integrable and

\[\mathbb E\langle b(Y_t),B_h-B_t\rangle=\left\langle\mathbb E b(Y_t),\mathbb E(B_h-B_t)\right\rangle=0.\]

The \(L^2\) inner product is this expectation. The state at time \(t\) depends only on initialization and noise up to \(t\). Composing with the drift observable preserves this dependence, while the increment over \([t,h]\) is independent and centered. This identity removes the contribution that an absolute norm bound would estimate at order \(\sqrt{h-t}\) in the subsequent energy comparison.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.title: Local smooth drift defect and the future cross term
ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.summary: Suppose the continuous Hilbert-valued reference satisfies \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\) with \(\|g(Y_t)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le\sigma\sqrt t\). Its increments are bounded by the sum of a term linear in time and a term proportional to the square root of time. The smooth drift’s Lipschitz constant then bounds its integrated local defect. For a bounded perturbation observable, first use orthogonality of the future noise; the remaining drift pairing is linear in the remaining time.

steps.title: The integrated smooth drift defect
steps.body:
The integral equation and the integral norm inequality give \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\). If \(a\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for \(0\le t\le h\), \(\|a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)\|\le L(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)\). Integration over length \(h\) therefore yields

\[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt ight\|\le Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h).\]

Equivalently, for solution \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\) with \(\|g(Y_s)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le u\sqrt t\), one has \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le tG+ u\sqrt t\). For smooth component \(a\) with Lipschitz constant \(L\), this gives

\[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt ight\|\le Lh(Gh+ u\sqrt h).\]

The estimate replaces both time factors by their endpoint maxima on \(0\le t\le h\), using monotonicity of \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\), and multiplies by interval length. Thus from \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\), multiplication by \(L\) controls the smooth force difference; for \(t\in[0,h]\) the factors \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\) are bounded by their endpoint values. Regularity may require Lipschitz continuity of the full drift, but only the smooth component’s constant enters this numerical bound.

steps.title: The future-drift pairing after noise orthogonality
steps.body:
Subtract the reference equations at \(t,h\) to obtain

\[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\]

If \(\|b\|\le K\) and \(\langle b,B_h-B_t\rangle=0\), the noise pairing is zero. Cauchy–Schwarz on the remaining drift integral gives \(\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le(h-t)GK\), avoiding an order-\(\sqrt{h-t}\) bound.

Splitting the integral at \(t\) gives the same difference identity

\[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\]

Pairing with \(b\) and applying orthogonality gives

\[\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le\left\|\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds\right\|\|b\|\le(h-t)GK.\]

In the application the inner product is in \(L^2\), so this cancellation is of the expected pairing. Subtraction at \(t\) and \(h\) leaves future drift integral of norm at most \((h-t)G\), hence remainder \((h-t)GK\). Brownian sample increments themselves do not vanish.

The subsequent comparison uses \(e\le f\) at the algorithm’s intermediate state and \(f\le e+\delta\) at the reference endpoint. The integrated gap is \(\delta\) because the source is a probability. All expected values are finite before subtraction, and no derivative of the original nonsmooth function is used.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.title: The synchronous one-step splitting estimate
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.summary: In the Hilbert space \(L^2\), suppose \(f_1\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let a Lipschitz map \(T\) satisfy the proximal energy inequality for \(f\). Assume the stationary reference satisfies the integral equation for \(f_1+e\) and \(e\le f\le e+\delta\), together with the stated moment and orthogonality conditions. Subtraction from the numerical forward step decomposes the discrepancy into a contractive smooth difference, a local smooth defect, and an integrated envelope force. steps.title: The four local forcing terms
steps.body:
For \(m,h>0\), drift bound \(G\), noise coefficient \(\sigma\), perturbation-gradient bound \(K\), and potential gap \(\delta\), set

\[\mathcal F=(1+(mh)^{-1})[Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)]^2+2h\delta+2h^2GK+h^2K^2.\]

The first term is the squared smooth local defect with Young factor \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). The other terms are, respectively, the finite potential-gap contribution, the reference drift paired with the bounded perturbation gradient, and the proximal quadratic remainder. These distinct estimates will bound the sum by a constant times the squared step.

steps.title: The error decomposition and energy comparison
steps.body:
Define \(S=X-h abla f_1(X)+B_h\), \(v=(X-h abla f_1(X))-(Y_0-h abla f_1(Y_0))\), \(R=\int_0^h[ abla f_1(Y_t)- abla f_1(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h abla e(Y_t)dt\). The shared noise and reference integral equation give \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). Expand its square and integrate the energy inequality for \(T(S)\). The expected \(f\) difference cancels with the corresponding force pairing up to the cross-energy bound. Smooth-step contraction and weighted Young control \(\|v+R\|^2\), while the local estimate controls \(R\). Discarding \(-\|H\|^2\le0\) gives

\[\|T(S)-Y_h\|_2^2\le(1-mh)\|X-Y_0\|_2^2+\mathcal F.\]

The conditions \(m\le L\) and \(h\le2/(m+L)\) imply \(mh\le1\), as required in the weighted contraction estimate. In the shorter notation \(a= abla f_1\), \(b= abla e\), \(S=X-ha(X)+B_h\), \(v=[X-ha(X)]-[Y_0-ha(Y_0)]\), \(R=\int_0^h[a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h b(Y_t)dt\), the exact difference is \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\) and its squared rearrangement is

\[\|S-Y_h\|^2=\|v+R\|^2+2\langle S-Y_h,H angle-\|H\|^2.\]

This identity retains the integrated envelope force until its energy comparison is applied. The nonpositive square can then be dropped. Weighted Young leaves coefficient \(1-mh\) on the preceding squared error. steps.title: The stationary comparison from an arbitrary finite-cost coupling
steps.body:
Let \(c\) be any finite-cost coupling of input law \(\mu\) and the Gibbs target. Its product with an independent Brownian probability space gives square-integrable initial variables with the prescribed marginals. The Langevin solution started at the target coordinate is stationary. Its adaptedness, future-increment independence, and moment bounds give

\[G=\sqrt{2L^2d/m+2K^2}+K,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{2d}.\]

The normalized increment over \([0,h]\) is independent standard Gaussian noise for the numerical transition. The resulting output pair is a finite-cost coupling, and the one-step theorem gives

\[W_2(\mu\mathcal T_h,\pi)^2\le(1-mh)\operatorname{cost}(c)^2+\mathcal F(m,h,L,G,\sigma,K,\delta).\]

More explicitly, the initial coupling \(c\) has reference marginal \(\pi\propto e^{-(f_1+e)}\) and gives initial variables \(X,Z\). The integral solution \(Y_t\) starts from \(Z\) and satisfies \(\operatorname{Law}(Y_t)=\pi\). Thus stationarity, Gaussian laws, moments, and orthogonality follow from the construction under the potential assumptions, rather than being extra assumptions of the final convergence theorem.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.title: The infimum of squared coupling estimates
ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.summary: Assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\) and \(q,c\ge0\). Suppose \(W_2(\mu', u')^2\le q\operatorname{cost}(p)^2+c\) holds for every finite-cost coupling \(p\) of \(\mu, u\). The same coefficient and forcing then bound the output squared Wasserstein distance in terms of the input squared distance. The proof below treats zero coefficients separately and otherwise uses the greatest-lower-bound property of the input cost infimum.

steps.title: The greatest-lower-bound argument
steps.body:
If \(q=0\), choose one finite-cost input coupling. If the output square is at most \(c\), nonnegativity of the other term already proves the claim. Otherwise the coefficient is positive and one may set \(r=\sqrt{(W_2(\mu', u')^2-c)/q}\). Each finite coupling estimate implies \(r\le\operatorname{cost}(p)\), and infinite-cost couplings satisfy the same extended lower bound. Hence \(r\le\inf_p\operatorname{cost}(p)=W_2(\mu, u)\). Squaring and multiplying by \(q\) gives

\[W_2(\mu', u')^2\le qW_2(\mu, u)^2+c.\]

In the notation \(A=W_2(\mu', u')^2\), the hypothesis is \(A\le qC^2+c\) for all finite costs. The case \(q=0\) gives \(A\le c\) directly. The case \(A\le c\) follows using \(q\ge0\). Otherwise \(r=\sqrt{(A-c)/q}\) is real and positive, and all coupling costs are at least \(r\).

Equivalently, costs may approach the finite infimum from above; continuity of squaring makes their squared costs tend to \(W_2(\mu, u)^2\). The fixed output bound survives that limit. These arguments require neither an optimal coupling nor division by a coefficient without first proving its positivity. One finite-cost comparison also establishes output finiteness.

steps.body:
The splitting law is the pushforward of its \(L^2\) iterate. Change of variables gives \(z\mapsto z\in L^2(\rho_n)\). Bounded parameter projection and subtraction of a constant give \(\theta(z)-a\in L^2(\rho_n)\) for every \(a\).

Indeed the \(L^2\) state is sent into \(L^2\) by the linear projection. A deterministic center is an \(L^2\) constant under a probability measure, so their difference has finite second moment. These moment conclusions hold for every positive proximal scale before the more restrictive convergence-step condition is imposed.

steps.title: Transport, equilibrium concentration, and center displacement
steps.body:
The smoothed target has sharp equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), and the uniform gap gives \(\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\). Projection of a coupling and Minkowski’s inequality therefore yield

\[\operatorname{RMS}_{\rho_n}(\theta_U)\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}+W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta}).\]

For algorithm law \(\rho_n\) and reference \(\Pi_{N,\eta}\), finite second moments ensure finite transport. The intermediate estimate is

\[R_{\theta_\eta}(\rho_n)\le W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}.\]

Changing the center by its deterministic displacement gives

\[R_{\theta_U}(\rho_n)\le W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}+\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}.\]

For each coupling the projection does not increase its quadratic cost, and the reference parameter error is bounded by \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\). Taking the coupling infimum gives the transport contribution. The center change is at most \(\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\) by the finite smoothing gap. These operations use the same smoothed target, and the subsequent splitting transport theorem supplies the remaining numerical bound.

ProximalLangevin/ProxParameter.lean.title: Sensitivity to the proximal parameter
ProximalLangevin/ProxParameter.lean.summary: For a convex bounded-below \(K\)-Lipschitz function, the proximal map satisfies \(\|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|\) at positive scales. The bound follows by representing one proximal point as a proximal point at the other scale with a shifted input. Jensen transfers this bound to the averaged particle map without an extra particle factor. Combined with common-innovation contraction, it gives finite-time and uniform-iteration comparisons of splitting chains at two scales.

steps.title: Value Lipschitzness from bounded supporting subgradients
steps.body:
Suppose a subgradient \(s_x\) is chosen at every point with \(\|s_x\|\le K\). Its support evaluated at \(y\) and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(f(x)-f(y)\le\langle s_x,x-y\rangle\le K\|x-y\|\). Exchange \(x,y\) to bound the absolute difference.

Thus a subgradient section bounded by \(K\) gives value Lipschitz constant \(K\). Every selected vector must satisfy the supporting inequality; the norm bound alone is insufficient. No derivative of the potential is required.

steps.title: Comparison of proximal minimizers at two positive scales
steps.body:
Write \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\). The residual characterization gives \(s\in\partial f(q)\) and \(\|s\|\le K\). The same support makes \(q\) the \(\lambda\)-proximal point of \(q+\lambda s\). Nonexpansiveness at scale \(\lambda\) yields

\[\|P_\lambda(x)-q\|\le\|x-(q+\lambda s)\|=|\eta-\lambda|\|s\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

In residual notation \(s=(x-P_\eta x)/\eta\), the second minimizer is also the \(\lambda\)-proximal point at \(P_\eta x+\lambda s\). Its comparison input is \(x=P_\eta x+\eta s\), so their separation is the scale difference times \(\|s\|\). The uniform residual bound gives \(K|\lambda-\eta|\) for every pair of positive scales.
steps.lean:
Let \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\). The optimality theorem gives \(s\in\partial f(q)\), and global value Lipschitzness gives \(\|s\|\le K\). Reversing the optimality characterization shows that the same \(q\) is \(P_\lambda(q+\lambda s)\). Nonexpansiveness at parameter \(\lambda\) therefore gives \[\|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le\|x-(q+\lambda s)\|=|\eta-\lambda|\|s\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|.\] The local identities hq, hxs and hid implement exactly these substitutions; both parameters must be positive to cancel their residual denominators.

steps.title: Uniform comparison of the averaged pair maps
steps.body:
Linearity in the supplied pair map gives \(\operatorname{Pair}_{P-Q}=\operatorname{Pair}_P-\operatorname{Pair}_Q\). If \(\sup_x\|P(x)-Q(x)\|\le c\), the averaged-square inequality bounds every summand by \(c^2\) and hence the state norm by \(c\). Proximal scale sensitivity therefore transfers with bound \(K|\lambda-\eta|\).

Explicitly \(\operatorname{Pair}(P-Q)=\operatorname{Pair}(P)-\operatorname{Pair}(Q)\). Under \(\|P(x)-Q(x)\|\le c\), Jensen and latent scaling give squared state difference at most \(N^{-1}\sum_i c^2=c^2\). Taking nonnegative square roots gives \(c\); substitute \(c=K|\lambda-\eta|\). Every pair difference is bounded by \(c\), and the state square is bounded by \(N^{-1}\sum_i c^2=c^2\), so the same constant \(c\) applies despite the common-parameter average.

steps.title: The finite-time and uniform scale-perturbation estimates
steps.body:
Insert an update at the first scale and the second current state. Common-innovation contraction controls the change of state, and proximal sensitivity controls the change of scale. Thus

\[e_{n+1}\le(1-m\gamma)e_n+K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

Induction gives \(e_n\le(1-m\gamma)^ne_0+K|\lambda-\eta|\sum_{j<n}(1-m\gamma)^j\). For \(\gamma>0\), the step restriction gives \(0\le1-m\gamma<1\), so the geometric sum is at most \(1/(m\gamma)\).

With intermediate input \(w\) and scale \(\lambda\) the same triangle inequality gives

\[e_{k+1}\le(1-m\gamma)e_k+K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

Under \(\gamma>0\), factor \(1-m\gamma<1\) gives floor \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). More precisely the two update changes are bounded by \(q e_k\) and \(K|\lambda-\eta|\). Summing under \(q=1-m\gamma<1\) yields \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). A common initialization removes the transient term. Since the innovations only need to agree, no distribution or independence assumption enters this pathwise estimate.

steps.title: A scale comparison within the specified interval
steps.body:
Suppose \(0<m\gamma<1\) and \(\gamma\le\lambda\le\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\). Subtraction gives \(|\lambda-\gamma|=\lambda-\gamma\le m\gamma^2/(1-m\gamma)\). Divide by positive \(m\gamma\) and multiply by \(K\) to obtain \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\le K\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\).

The width of the allowed scale interval is \(\gamma/(1-m\gamma)-\gamma=m\gamma^2/(1-m\gamma)\). Its lower endpoint \(\gamma\) makes the absolute difference from the reference scale equal to the nonnegative difference. Division by \(m\gamma>0\) gives the bound. The strict condition \(m\gamma<1\) is required because the denominator vanishes at equality.

This term measures the additional error incurred by changing the proximal parameter away from the equal-step algorithm.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingTheorem.lean.title: PIPGLA about the original center for every positive proximal scale
ProximalLangevin/SplittingTheorem.lean.summary: Assume the stated strong convexity and smoothness of \(g_1\), and convexity, a lower bound, and \(K\)-Lipschitz values for \(g_2\). Let \(N>0\), \(0<m\le L_1\), \(\lambda,\gamma>0\), and \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_1)\). Initialization belongs to \(L^2\) and all Gaussian innovation coordinates are mutually independent and independent of initialization. Compare the chain at its chosen proximal scale with the equal-step chain. Its transport bound, parameter concentration, and finite center displacement then give the error estimate relative to the original marginal maximizer with the scale-mismatch contribution retained.

steps.title: The root mean square comparison of two scales
steps.body:
Use the same initial variable and innovations for the \(\lambda\) and \(\eta\) chains. Their uniform state separation is at most \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). Parameter projection is nonexpansive, and both chains have finite second moments. Minkowski therefore gives

\[\operatorname{RMS}_\lambda(a)\le\operatorname{RMS}_\eta(a)+\frac{K|\lambda-\eta|}{m\gamma}.\]

This is an inequality for their \(L^2\) realizations. More explicitly, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the \(L^2\) iterates at scales \(\lambda\) and \(\eta\). The pathwise bound is

\[\|X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\|\le c:=\frac{K|\lambda-\eta|}{m\gamma}\quad\text{almost surely}.\]

Its \(L^2\) norm is at most the same constant because the source has mass one. Projection followed by Minkowski adds the reference-center error. Pushforward integration identifies the two ordinary law integrals, both finite by the moment result.

pipgla_parameter_rms_prox_comparison constructs the two square-integrable chains X and Y on the same probability space and the comparison radius c. hpoint uses pipglaChain_parameter_comparison_bound at common initial input, and hXY integrates the resulting pointwise bound. The centered projected vectors A and B satisfy hAB; projection contraction and the triangle inequality give hn. hnorm identifies each law-based root integral with its corresponding Hilbert-space norm using pipglaLaws_eq_lpLaw, integral_map and lp_norm_sq_eq_integral. Both proximal scales are positive; this comparison does not require the noises themselves to be independent Gaussian vectors.

The transient term vanishes because both initial states agree. The full-measure representative equalities for the two chains and their subtraction justify this substitution in hpoint. Since \(Q\) has total mass one, integrating the uniform bound gives \(\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\le c\); this is hXY.

Define \(A=P_\theta X-\theta\) and \(B=P_\theta Y-\theta\) as \(L^2\) variables. Linearity gives \(A-B=P_\theta(X-Y)\), and the projection norm bound gives \(\|A-B\|_2\le\|X-Y\|_2\). Thus \(\|A\|_2\le\|B\|_2+c\), the inequality hn. Finally, hnorm first identifies each actual law as the pushforward of its \(L^2\) iterate, then changes variables in the quadratic integral and uses \(\sqrt{\|A\|_2^2}=\|A\|_2\). All these norms are finite by construction. Substituting those two identities into hn proves the stated RMS comparison.

steps.title: The PIPGLA estimate about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Choose comparison scale \(\eta=\gamma\). The equal-step transport estimate and parameter projection relative to the original marginal maximizer give

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{RMS}_\lambda(\theta_U)\le{}&\frac{K|\lambda-\gamma|}{m\gamma}+\sqrt{\frac{\gamma K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\&+\sqrt{(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2+\frac\gamma N C_N}.\end{aligned}\]

The explicit finite coefficient \(C_N\) is independent of the forward step. Every positive \(\lambda\) is allowed, with its displayed mismatch term. Convergence as \(\gamma\to0\) additionally requires control of that term. The coefficient is the proved one and does not reproduce the source’s printed heat-flow constants.

At reference scale \(\gamma\), the transport estimate gives the square root of the transient squared distance plus its floor. Sharp equilibrium concentration and the finite smoothing displacement add the other terms. For chosen scale \(\lambda\), common-innovation sensitivity gives \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\). Its constant bound has the same root mean square value under a probability source, giving the addition \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\). Thus allowance of all positive \(\lambda\) is distinct from a bound uniform as the forward step tends to zero. The preceding scale-interval estimate gives a simpler mismatch bound when that interval condition holds.

ProximalLangevin/Recurrence.lean.title: Scalar affine recurrences for the proposed splitting coefficients
ProximalLangevin/Recurrence.lean.summary:
Assume a scalar affine inequality with the coefficients specified below. Nonnegative multiplication and induction give its finite geometric sum. A strict ratio below one gives a uniform error bound; ratio one gives only the finite-horizon linear bound. These are conditional scalar conclusions. A stochastic one-step estimate must be proved separately before this recurrence can describe an algorithmic error.

This file proves scalar consequences of an explicitly supplied recurrence. It does not supply the stochastic one-step law estimate for the paper’s coefficient. The independently proved PIPGLA law theorem uses the constructed coupling route.

steps.title: The proposed coefficients and their sign conditions
steps.body:
Define

\[q=\frac{\lambda(1-\mu\gamma)}\gamma,\qquad c=\lambda\left(\frac{2\gamma LD}{N}+\lambda C\right).\]

The stated sign assumptions give \(q,c\ge0\). Under \(\gamma>0\) and \(\mu\gamma<1\), multiplication through positive denominators gives \(q<1\iff\lambda<\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\). The strict inequality is needed for the geometric denominator. The subgradient contribution is \(\lambda^2C\) and has no further division by \(N\).

Equivalently let \(q=\lambda(1-\mu\gamma)/\gamma\) and \(c=2\lambda\gamma LD/N+\lambda^2C\). Positivity of \(\gamma\) and \(1-\mu\gamma\) makes \(q<1\) equivalent to \(\lambda<\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\). Division by \(1-q\) is consequently permitted only under that strict condition; the signs of \(q,c\) follow separately. In particular \(q<1\) fails at the limiting scale, where \(q=1\). Only the Gaussian part of the forcing contains \(1/N\), so its particle scaling differs from the subgradient part.

steps.title: The finite geometric bound for an assumed recurrence
steps.body:
Assume \(e_{n+1}\le q e_n+c\) and \(q\ge0\). Repeated substitution gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+c\sum_{j<n}q^j\). If \(q<1\), the finite geometric identity gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+c(1-q^n)/(1-q)\). Under \(c\ge0\) the tail term \(-cq^n/(1-q)\) is nonpositive, so \(e_n\le q^ne_0+c/(1-q)\).

The induction is over \(n\). Multiply the preceding bound by nonnegative \(q\) and add \(c\). When \(q<1\) the geometric denominator is positive; when \(c\ge0\) its negative tail may be discarded. Each statement keeps the original recurrence as an explicit hypothesis.

ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.title: Exact algebraic corrections and an averaged-proximity counterexample
ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.summary:
The examples below establish specific algebraic facts used to qualify the source arguments: the sign of a quadratic proximal expansion, scaling of a squared norm, the inverse-step factor in residual monotonicity, and failure of shared-state proximal optimality for averaged pairwise outputs. The convergence results use the finite potential-gap and summed energy inequalities proved above. Each example has only the scope stated for its own assumptions.

This module contains explicit mathematical certificates. Each claim is limited to its stated algebraic example or implication; these certificates do not claim that every stronger result in the reference paper is false.

steps.title: The second-order sign in the quadratic proximal expansion
steps.body:
The proximal equation \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second-order coefficient in the scalar quadratic example:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative coefficient printed in the source leaves error at least \(\lambda^2\) at \(x=1\) and therefore cannot be its third-order expansion. The quadratic is not globally value Lipschitz, so this calculation diagnoses the displayed algebra rather than refuting a full theorem under that assumption.

Almost-everywhere twice differentiability and the stated moment condition also do not provide the uniform integrable third-order remainder needed for the claimed order \(O(\lambda)\) for displacement of the original marginal maximizer. The proved finite-gap result gives \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\); this difference in established scope does not prove the stronger assertion false. For \(f(u)=u^2/2\) the minimizer equation is \((1+\lambda)p=x\). Division gives the exact resolvent and its positive \(\lambda^2x\) term with the displayed third-order remainder.

steps.title: The inverse-step factor in residual monotonicity
steps.body:
Assume \(\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle\le(1-\mu)\|x-y\|^2\) and define the residual difference by \(R(x)-R(y)=\gamma^{-1}[(x-y)-(p(x)-p(y))]\). For \(\gamma>0\), expansion gives \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\ge(\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). Hence the strong-monotonicity coefficient is \(\mu/\gamma\) rather than \(\mu\).

Explicitly the inner product expands as \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle=\gamma^{-1}(\|x-y\|^2-\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle)\). Substitution of the proximal deficit bounds it below by \((\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). Division by \(\gamma\) in the residual definition is the source of this inverse-step factor.

steps.title: A counterexample to shared-state proximal optimality
steps.body:
Take \(g(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\) and proximal scale one. The pair inputs \((1,0)\) and \((1,4)\) have proximal minimizers \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The shared-state objective is

\[\tfrac12(|\theta-x_1|+|\theta-x_2|)+\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2+\tfrac14(x_1^2+(x_2-4)^2).\]

The competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller objective, as follows from direct absolute-value evaluation. Each pair was allowed its own proposed parameter, whereas the shared objective permits only one. Averaging the proposals need not solve that common minimization problem.

In particular the averaged output has value \(51/32\) and the feasible comparator has value \(3/2=48/32\). This strict comparison disproves the shared-state proximal identity in general. The splitting proof instead sums the valid single-pair energy inequalities and applies Jensen’s inequality to the parameter average.

The quadratic penalty uses precisely the scaled state norm with \(N=2\). averaged_pair_prox_not_lifted_minimizer : Averaging the two true pairwise proximal outputs gives parameter \(5/4\) and particles \((1/2,3)\). A feasible competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller lifted objective. Thus the pairwise average cannot be a lifted proximal minimizer, even for a convex globally Lipschitz penalty.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.title: Wasserstein regularity of the integrated parameter force
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.summary: For pair potential \(V\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, define the parameter force by \(b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\mu(dx)\). Finite latent second moments and linear gradient growth make this a Bochner integral. Comparing the integrands on arbitrary couplings gives a bound in quadratic Wasserstein distance. Parameter projection is a contraction, so the joint-gradient regularity constant also controls this force.

steps.title: Expectation differences for a Lipschitz observable
steps.body:
For a Lipschitz observable \(\phi\), subtract \(\phi(0)\). Its centered growth is bounded by \(K\|x\|\), giving \(\phi(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). For any finite-cost coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\), the norm-of-integral inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz give

\[\left\|\int\phi\,d\mu-\int\phi\,d u ight\|\le K\left(\int\|x-y\|^2dc ight)^{1/2}.\]

The infimum of coupling costs gives \(K W_2(\mu, u)\). The coupling integral identity is

\[\int\varphi\,d\mu-\int\varphi\,d u=\int[\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)]\,dc(x,y).\]

Integrability includes the observable’s value at zero. Its Lipschitz constant bounds the integrand difference by the pair distance, and \(\|\cdot\|_1\le\|\cdot\|_2\) bounds its first moment by its quadratic cost. The input second moments make the infimum finite; no optimal coupling is required.
steps.lean:
The nonzero value \(\varphi(0)\) must be retained when proving integrability. Write \(\varphi(X)=[\varphi(X)-\varphi(0)]+\varphi(0)\). The first term is in \(L^2\) because its Lipschitz map vanishes at zero; the second is a constant in \(L^2\) on a probability space. This proves memLp_lipschitz_observable, including the offset.

For the transport estimate, take any coupling \(c\) of \(\mu,\nu\). Its marginal identities pull the given second moments onto its two coordinate random variables. Applying the observable lemma to both coordinates proves their \(L^2\) membership and hence their Bochner integrability. The fact hid then changes variables using those marginals and combines the two integrals:

The successive inequalities in hfamily are the integral triangle inequality, the probability-space comparison \(\|F\|_1\le\|F\|_2\), and the pointwise Lipschitz bound \(\|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\|\le K\|x-y\|\). They give the same upper bound \(K\,\operatorname{cost}(c)\) for every coupling. Taking the infimum in the extended nonnegative reals proves hbound. Finite input second moments already imply finite \(W_2\), so the product \(KW_2\) is finite and the final conversion to real numbers preserves the inequality.

steps.title: The parameter block of the joint gradient
steps.body:
The orthogonal projection \(P_\theta\) keeps the parameter coordinates and satisfies \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\) because their squared norm is a subsum of the full squared norm. Define \(\phi_\theta(x)=P_\theta\nabla V(\theta,x)\) and integrate this observable against the latent law.

It is the integrated parameter block of the specified potential gradient, rather than an independently assumed vector field.

steps.title: The two-coordinate gradient perturbation bound
steps.body:
Decomposing the pair difference into parameter and latent inclusions gives \(\|(\theta,x)-(\theta',x')\|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|\). The joint-gradient Lipschitz estimate followed by the parameter contraction gives

\[\|\phi_\theta(x)-\phi_{\theta'}(x')\|\le L(\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|).\]

For \(\theta=\theta'\) the latent observable is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Fixing the latent coordinate similarly gives the separate parameter bound. The sum on the right comes from the triangle inequality on the two orthogonal coordinate inclusions.

steps.title: Separate parameter and probability-law perturbations
steps.body:
For differentiable \(V\) define

\[ b_V( heta,\mu)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \( abla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu, u\) have finite second moments. Linear growth gives integrability. Comparison on a finite-cost coupling, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the cost infimum then give

\[ \|b_V( heta,\mu)-b_V( heta', u)\| \le L igl(\| heta- heta'\|+W_2(\mu, u) igr). \]

For split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) the gradient constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The source’s \(1/\eta\) constant is the full-envelope constant and is not in general sufficient for this split potential. Moreover the present estimate is in quadratic Wasserstein distance, a weaker conclusion than the source’s first-Wasserstein assertion. It does not alone establish the later propositions cited there.

For arbitrary coupling \((X,Y)\), the \(L\)-Lipschitz joint gradient gives \(\| abla_ heta U( heta,x)- abla_ heta U(\vartheta,y)\|\le L(\| heta-\vartheta\|+\|x-y\|)\). Integration and Cauchy–Schwarz on \(\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\) yield

\[\|b( heta,\mu)-b(\vartheta, u)\|\le L\| heta-\vartheta\|+LW_2(\mu, u).\]

The Moreau substitution gives \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). Alternatively insert intermediate force \(b_V( heta',\mu)\): its parameter change is at most \(L\| heta- heta'\|\) and its law change at most \(LW_2(\mu, u)\). Their sum proves the claim with constant \(L_1+1/\eta\) for split smoothing.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.title: Mean-field integral equations in the space of square-integrable states
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.summary: On probability space \(Q\) let \(H=L^2(Q;\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x})\). A potential \(V\) with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient induces a Lipschitz composition map on this Hilbert space. A bounded linear operator replaces only its parameter component by expectation. Picard’s theorem constructs the integral solution with a continuous additive input. Projection gives a deterministic parameter equation coupled to the law of the latent component when the initial parameter is deterministic and the input is latent-only.

steps.title: Expectation as a bounded linear map
steps.body:
Under a probability measure, \(\|X\|_{L^1}\le\|X\|_{L^2}\). The norm-of-integral inequality therefore gives \(\|\mathbb E_Q X\|\le\|X\|_2\). Bochner integration is linear on these integrable variables, defining continuous linear map \(\mathcal E:H\to E\) with operator norm at most one.

Continuity makes expectation commute with continuous time integrals. This fact will identify the deterministic parameter equation after projecting the joint Hilbert-space solution.

steps.title: Coordinate projections and parameter inclusion
steps.body:
Define latent projection \(P_x(\theta,x)=x\) and parameter inclusion \(I_\theta(\theta)=(\theta,0)\). Coordinate expansion gives \(\|(\theta,0)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2\), so \(I_\theta\) is an isometry. Both maps are bounded and linear, and their pointwise actions preserve these properties on square-integrable random vectors. They consequently commute with the Bochner time integrals in the projected equations.

steps.title: The parameter-averaging operator
steps.body:
Define the bounded linear averaging operator by

\[\mathcal M X=\operatorname{const}(I_\theta P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)+M_xX.\]

The norm of each summand is at most \(\|X\|_2\), so \(\|\mathcal M X\|_2\le2\|X\|_2\). Linearity gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal M)\le2\). This sufficient constant is not asserted optimal.

The operator sends a joint state \((\Theta,X)\) to \((\mathbb E\Theta,X)\), where the first component is represented as a constant random vector. Only the parameter component is averaged. The latent force remains a random function of its current latent state, as required for the mean-field system.

steps.title: The mean-field drift and finite-horizon integral solution
steps.body:
Set \(\mathcal A_V(X)=\mathcal M(\nabla V(X))\). Composition with the Lipschitz gradient preserves \(L^2\) and has constant \(L\). The averaging bound gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). For a continuous \(H\)-valued input \(B\) satisfying \(B_0=0\) and any \(T\ge0\), Picard’s theorem gives continuous \(Y\) with \(Y_0=Y^{\rm in}\) and

\[Y_t-Y^{\rm in}=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)ds+B_t,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The complete space is \(H\). Writing \(E=\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\), expectation is a bounded linear map \(L^2(Q;E)\to E\). Constant inclusion maps \(E\) back into \(H=L^2(Q;E)\). Composing these maps with the parameter projection averages the parameter component; the latent component is left unchanged. The coordinate maps are bounded. Linear growth makes gradient composition everywhere defined on \(L^2\), so the averaged drift has constant at most \(2L\). Subtracting the continuous additive input reduces the equation to a nonautonomous globally Lipschitz integral equation. This proves finite-horizon existence and the displayed identity from the stated input and potential assumptions.

steps.title: The deterministic parameter and latent integral equations
steps.body:
Assume initial parameter \(\theta_0\) is constant and \(P_\theta B_t=0\). Projection commutes with the time integral, giving \(P_\theta Y_t=\operatorname{const}(\theta_t)\) where \(\theta_t=\theta_0-\int_0^t a_V(Y_s)ds\). Continuity of the primitive proves continuity of \(\theta\). Define \(\mu_t=\mathcal L_Q(P_xY_t)\) and substitute the force identity:

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t b_V(\theta_s,\mu_s)ds,\qquad P_xY_t-P_xY_0=-\int_0^tP_x\nabla V(Y_s)ds+P_xB_t.\]

The latent equality is in \(L^2\). The parameter input is zero and the parameter drift is constant as a random vector, so its time integral is constant as well. Thus the deterministic path \(\theta_t\) is derived from the joint solution. In terms of its latent law \(\mu_t\), the equation is

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t\left[\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta_s,x)\,d\mu_s(x)\right]ds.\]

Latent projection gives the drift-plus-noise equation in the display. Both equations use the same constructed process and its latent distribution.

Assume additionally that the convex penalty is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. Its proximal residual then equals the original gradient evaluated at the proximal point. The finite proximal displacement bounds the difference between original and envelope gradients by a constant times the smoothing scale. Construct both mean-field integral solutions with identical initial state and additive input. The input cancels on subtraction, and Grönwall bounds the supremum over time of their mean-square norms.

For this module the convex bounded-below \(g_2\) is additionally differentiable, with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient and global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The finite-horizon comparison uses the same initialization and additive input for the original and split-smoothed systems.

steps.title: Equality of the subgradient and gradient at a differentiability point
steps.body:
If \(s\) is a supporting subgradient, then \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) has a global minimum at \(p\). Differentiability makes its derivative zero, giving \(s= abla f(p)\). Applied to the proximal residual and envelope-gradient formula, this gives \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta(x))\).

Equivalently, a support \(s\) at \(p\) minimizes \(f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) at \(p\), so \(s= abla f(p)\). The conclusion is an equality at the minimizing point, not an asymptotic approximation.

steps.title: The finite gradient difference under smoothing
steps.body:
The gradient \( abla f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz, and \(P_\eta\) is nonexpansive. Their composition therefore has constant \(L_2\) independently of \(\eta\). The displacement bound \(\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta K\) then gives

\[\| abla f(x)- abla f^\eta(x)\|\le L_2\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

Optimality and differentiability identify \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta x)\). When \( abla f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz and \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, the same argument gives

\[\| abla f^\eta(x)- abla f(x)\|\le L_2\|P_\eta x-x\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

The envelope gradient is \( abla f\circ P_\eta\). Its gradient constant is bounded by \(L_2\), which can be smaller than the generic \(1/\eta\) bound. Comparison with \( abla f(x)\) costs at most \(L_2\|P_\eta x-x\|\le\eta L_2K\). This finite uniform defect supplies the forcing in the integral-equation comparison.

steps.title: Component regularity from the sum and the smooth term
steps.body:
If \(U=f+g\) and \(f\) are differentiable, then \(g=U-f\) is differentiable. Gradient linearity gives \( abla g= abla U- abla f\). Taking differences at two points and the triangle inequality yields \(\operatorname{Lip}( abla g)\le L_U+L_f\).

Thus the constant \(L_2\) may be supplied from regularity of the original sum and the known smooth component. This gives a justified \(L_2\) without adding an unstated differentiability assumption on the remaining component.

steps.title: Comparison with common additive input
steps.body:
Let integral solutions with drifts \(g,k\) share additive input \(B\) and have initial states \(x,y\). Assume one drift is globally Lipschitz and \(\sup_z\|g(z)-k(z)\|\le\varepsilon\). Subtraction cancels the input. Adding and subtracting one drift at the other state bounds the integrand by \(L\|Y-Z\|+\varepsilon\). Integral Grönwall gives

\[\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le e^{Lt}\|x-y\|+\varepsilon\Psi(L,t),\qquad\Psi(L,t)=\begin{cases}(e^{Lt}-1)/L,&L\ne0,\\t,&L=0.\end{cases}\]

No differentiation of \(B\) is needed. The bounded defect is integrated with factor \(\Psi\). The definition of \(\Psi\) includes zero Lipschitz constant, so the formula requires no division by zero.

steps.title: The finite smoothing estimate for the two integral systems
steps.body:
Assume \(g_2\) is differentiable with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient, and retain convexity, a lower bound, and value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The supporting residual equals the gradient at the proximal minimizer:

\[ \nabla g_2^\eta(v)=\nabla g_2(P_\eta(v)). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P_\eta\) preserves constant \(L_2\), and \(\|v-P_\eta(v)\|\le\eta K\) gives

\[ \|\nabla g_2(v)-\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\|\le\eta L_2K. \]

If instead regularity is stated for \(U=g_1+g_2\) with constant \(L_U\) and for \(g_1\) with constant \(L_1\), the difference argument supplies \(L_2=L_U+L_1\).

Construct both Hilbert-space solutions with common initial state and continuous additive input. The averaged drifts differ uniformly by at most \(2\eta L_2K\). Their pair-gradient constant is at most \(L_1+L_2\), independent of \(\eta\). The averaging operator gives the corresponding factor two. Grönwall yields

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|Y_t-Z_t\|_{L^2} \le 2\eta L_2K\,\Psi(2(L_1+L_2),T), \qquad \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0.\end{cases} \]

For deterministic initial parameter and latent-only Brownian input these are the mean-field systems described above. The finite bound is linear in \(\eta\). More explicitly the averaged drift constant is \(2(L_1+L_2)\) and its uniform difference is \(2\eta L_2K\). The supremum is outside the \(L^2\) norm. Proposition C.3 instead bounds the expectation of the supremum of squared errors. The square root of that quantity bounds the supremum of the \(L^2\) error norms. A bound on the expectation of the supremum of squared errors is not established here.

One drift contributes its global Lipschitz constant times the current difference; the other contributes the uniform Moreau score defect just proved. Grönwall then bounds the actual process difference by a coefficient times \(\eta\) on the finite horizon. The component-regularity declarations justify the smoothness constants of each summand from the stated assumptions on the regular sum before this perturbation argument is applied.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.title: Exact iid variance and the empirical parameter force
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.summary: For \(N>0\), independent centered square-integrable Hilbert-valued vectors have zero mixed expected inner products. Expanding the finite squared sum and integrating termwise therefore gives an exact \(1/N\) variance factor for their sample mean. The finite product measure supplies the required independence. Applying the identity to the parameter-gradient observable gives the empirical mean-field force fluctuation.

steps.title: The centered off-diagonal expectations
steps.body:
View the supplied \(L^2\) functions as \(L^2\) vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz makes each pairwise inner product integrable, so finite expansion gives

\[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_iX_i\right\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j\rangle.\]

For \(i\ne j\), independence and zero means give \(\langle\mathbb E X_i,\mathbb E X_j\rangle=0\). The diagonal terms are \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). For distinct indices \(i\ne j\), centering alone would not remove covariance; independence is required for this factorization. Products of \(L^2\) norms are integrable, which justifies the complete termwise identity.
steps.lean:
Expand the Hilbert square as \(\|\sum_iX_i\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\). Each mixed product is integrable by the \(L^2\) inner-product bound, which justifies moving the finite double sum through the integral. For \(i\ne j\), independence factors \(\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) into \(\langle\mathbb EX_i,\mathbb EX_j\rangle=0\). For \(i=j\), it is \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). The local facts hint, hcross and hexpand establish these prerequisites and identities separately. Centering without independence would leave the off-diagonal covariances.

steps.title: The variance of an independent sample mean
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\) and let \(\phi\) be square-integrable under probability \(\mu\). On \(\mu^{\otimes N}\) the coordinate samples are independent. Center \(\phi\) by its expectation, expand the squared sample mean, and cancel its off-diagonal pairings. This gives

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

The root mean square sampling factor is \(N^{-1/2}\). This variance identity is an ingredient in particle comparison, not by itself a propagation-of-chaos theorem. Exchangeability alone would not cancel covariances.

Indeed let \(C_i=\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E\phi\). Its average is \(N^{-1}\sum_iC_i\), the expected squared sum is \(N\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\), and the averaging prefactor is \(N^{-2}\). Their product is \(N^{-1}\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\). Taking square roots gives \(1/\sqrt N\). Independence here comes from the finite product construction, rather than an assumption about interacting particle states.
steps.lean:
On the explicit product probability \(P=\mu^{\otimes N}\), set \(C(a)=\varphi(a)-\mathbb E_\mu\varphi\) and \(X_i(\omega)=C(\omega_i)\). Measure-preserving coordinate evaluation proves that each \(X_i\) has the same finite second moment, zero mean and law, and the product construction proves their joint independence. The exact centered-mean identity is \[\frac1N\sum_i\varphi(\omega_i)-\mathbb E\varphi=\frac1N\sum_iX_i(\omega).\] Thus the previous variance identity gives \[\mathbb E_P\left\|\frac1N\sum_i\varphi(\omega_i)-\mathbb E\varphi\right\|^2=\frac{\mathbb E_\mu\|\varphi-\mathbb E\varphi\|^2}{N}.\] In the code, hXi, hind, hmean, hvar and hid verify each of these assertions. Taking the nonnegative square root gives the RMS version.

steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\), fix \( heta\), and put \(\phi(x)= abla_ heta U( heta,x)\). Its expectation is \(b_U( heta,\mu)\). The independent-sample identity therefore gives

\[\mathbb E\left\| rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,X_i)-b_U( heta,\mu) ight\|^2= rac1N\mathbb E\| abla_ heta U( heta,X)-b_U( heta,\mu)\|^2.\]

This is the exact variance of the empirical parameter force. Its finite variance is derived from the gradient and latent-moment assumptions rather than postulated as an additional sampling-error bound.

steps.title: Coordinate inclusions and square-integrable contractions
steps.body:
Define the latent inclusion \(I_x(x)=(0,x)\). Adding zero parameter coordinates gives \(\|I_xx\|=\|x\|\), and latent projection has norm at most one. For a pointwise linear contraction \(C\), integration of \(\|C(X)\|^2\le\|X\|^2\) gives \(\|C\circ X\|_2\le\|X\|_2\).

Thus coordinate inclusion and projection are contractions also in \(L^2\). They introduce no dimension factor in reconstruction of the random pair. The maximum product norm consequently controls every parameter and tagged latent-coordinate difference.

steps.title: Particle-count-independent Lipschitzness and the integral solution
steps.body:
Every coordinate difference is bounded by the maximum product distance, so pair reconstruction and gradient regularity give \(\|\nabla V(J_i z)-\nabla V(J_i w)\|_2\le2L\|z-w\|\). Averaging the \(N\) parameter terms and dividing by \(N>0\) preserves this bound. The maximum latent-coordinate norm preserves it as well. Hence \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_N)\le2L\) independently of \(N\). Picard gives continuous \(Z\) satisfying \(Z_t-Z_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_N(Z_s)ds+B_t\) for continuous input with \(B_0=0\).

The state consists of one parameter \(L^2\) vector and finitely many latent \(L^2\) vectors. For particle \(i\), reconstruction gives \(\|\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x_i)-\operatorname{pair}(\vartheta,y_i)\|_2\le\|\theta-\vartheta\|_2+\|x_i-y_i\|_2\le2\|z-w\|\). The \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient therefore bounds its force difference by \(2L\|z-w\|\). Averaging cancels factor \(N\) and gives constant \(2L\). Equivalently the reconstruction factor two is multiplied by \(L\); averaging \(N\) parameter bounds and taking the maximum of latent bounds leaves \(2L\). The finite-horizon integral equation follows from completeness and global drift Lipschitzness.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.title: Independent copies and the empirical parameter-force residual

steps.title: Reconstruction and drift composition for copied pairs
steps.body:
Recombining the parameter and latent projections recovers the original \(L^2\) vector. For deterministic parameter this gives \(J_i\mathcal R_N(X)=C_iX\). Composition of the copied state with a Lipschitz pointwise drift is the same as copying the composition, since both representatives equal \(b(X(\omega_i))\) almost surely.

For the gradient, this common representative is \(\nabla V(X(\omega_i))\). Hence each reconstructed reference pair has precisely the copied joint drift. This equality causes the latent components to cancel in the particle-minus-reference drift.

steps.title: The empirical parameter-force drift residual
steps.body:
Apply the particle drift to \(\mathcal R_N(X)\) and compare it with \(\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_V(X))\). Reconstruction and gradient commutation identify all latent components, leaving

\[\mathcal A_N(\mathcal R_NX)-\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_VX)=\left(\Delta_N(P_ heta abla V(X)),0 ight).\]

The maximum product norm and sample-mean variance identity give residual norm \(\|\mathcal C(P_ heta abla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). In detail, latent coordinate \(i\) combines with the deterministic parameter to recover joint copy \(i\). The parameter discrepancy is

\[ rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta V( heta,X_i)-\mathbb E abla_ heta V( heta,X).\]

It is the empirical parameter force minus its expectation. Its norm is the centered single-copy force norm divided by \(\sqrt N\), equivalently \(\|\mathcal C(P_ heta abla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). This exact residual supplies the sampling forcing used in the comparison theorem.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.title: Grönwall comparison with an extra continuous noise input
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.summary: A common sampling factor gives an \(N^{-1/2}\) comparison for an integral drift defect and an additional continuous input. In a Banach space let \(F\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Compare two integral equations with common input \(B\), additional input \(A\) in one equation, and reference drift \(G\). Subtracting the additional input before applying Grönwall yields a differentiable remainder without differentiating either noise path.

steps.title: The difference after subtraction of the additional input
steps.body:
Let \(L\ge0\) and \(T\ge0\), and define \(\Psi(L,T)=\int_0^T e^{L(T-s)}ds\). Thus \(\Psi(0,T)=T\), and \(\Psi(L,T)=(e^{LT}-1)/L\) for \(L>0\). Assume \(\|A_t\|\le a\), \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), and

\[X_t-x=-\int_0^tF(X_s)ds+B_t+A_t,\qquad Y_t-x=-\int_0^tG_sds+B_t.\]

Put \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\). Subtraction cancels the common input, and the Lipschitz and defect bounds give \(\|D_t\|\le\int_0^t[L\|D_s\|+La+C]ds\). Grönwall then yields \(\|X_t-Y_t\|\le(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a\) on \([0,T]\).

The continuous inputs \(B,A\) may be Brownian inputs in \(L^2\). Defining \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\) cancels \(B\) and \(A\) algebraically and leaves

\[D_t=-\int_0^t[F(X_s)-G_s]ds,\quad D_0=0.\]

Continuity of the integrand makes this remainder differentiable with derivative \(-F(X_t)+G_t\). Equivalently, for \(D=X-Y-A\), the remainder \(D\) is differentiable although \(A\) need not be. Since \(X-Y=D+A\), its derivative is bounded by \(L\|D\|+La+C\). Grönwall bounds \(D\), and restoring \(A\) adds \(a\). This proves the estimate using only continuous integral equations.
steps.lean:
If \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(\|A_t\|\le a\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), then \[\|D'_t\|\le L\|D_t\|+C+La.\] The right-derivative Grönwall theorem gives \(\|D_t\|\le\operatorname{gronwallBound}(0,L,C+La,T)\) uniformly on \([0,T]\). Adding back \(A_t\) produces the final \(+a\). In Lean, hDI identifies the differentiable integral remainder, hderiv proves its derivative, and hb establishes this exact scalar forcing.

Formal correspondence: integral_forcing_perturbation : Actual integral equations with common input, an additional continuous input, and a uniformly controlled reference-force defect satisfy this finite-horizon bound. Neither a derivative of the input nor an error recurrence is assumed.

steps.title: The comparison with a common inverse sampling factor
steps.body:
The zero-initial-error Grönwall bound is \(C\Psi(L,T)\), where \(\Psi\) is defined above. It is linear in \(C\), including when \(L=0\). Let \(r>0\) and suppose that \(\|A_t\|\le a/r\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C/r\) throughout the interval. Substitution in the preceding bound gives

\[\|X_t-Y_t\|\le\frac{(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a}{r}.\]

Indeed, the differential inequality for the remainder has forcing \(C/r+La/r=(C+La)/r\). Grönwall multiplies this forcing by \(\Psi(L,T)\), and restoring the additional input contributes \(a/r\). For \(r=\sqrt N\), with \(N>0\), the resulting coefficient is independent of \(N\) whenever \(C,L,a,T\) are independent of \(N\).
